Mr. Chairman, with a good deal of what has been said by the speakers in this debate I am sure that we in this corner can find ourselves substantially in agreement. With a good deal of what has been said by the leader of the C.C.F. group, I am afraid we would have to take issue. In the course of what I shall say this afternoon in connection with the resolution now before us, I shall point out one or two of those more important things upon which we have to differ from my hon. friend, the leader of the C.C.F.
I turn now to the resolution. The language of the resolution that we are discussing today is like a velvet glove on a mailed fist. The language is bland and considerate and it makes it appear that the federal government is generous and thoughtful in its dealings with the provinces. But underneath a number of very dulcet phrases such as "the minister may pay to a province out of the consolidated revenue fund", "tax equalization payment", "provincial revenue stabilization payment" and "tax rental agreement as an alternative to levying such taxes on its own behalf"-as I say, under these,

which I am sure are dulcet phrases to the provinces-there is to be found by careful study evidence of a surprisingly hard and uncompromising attitude on the part of the government of Canada.
I thoroughly agree with what has already been said in this debate to the effect that certain principles enunciated in the resolution are good and must carry a good deal of comfort to those provinces which have not had a reasonable deal ever since the days of confederation and where, as my hon. friend from Rosetown-Biggar has pointed out, there is the need for equalization payments. Recognition of that need is set out in the resolution, and we agree that recognition of the principle of equalization grants is something that has been long overdue and is something with which we must agree. So there are some things in the resolution that we regard as good; and we are pleased to see the government's acceptance of the principles contained in those phrases about which I have spoken briefly.
If we were to judge solely by the resolution that is before us and by what the Minister of Finance said in his speech this morning we would doubtless have to agree that this government was trying to be fair and just in its dealings with the provinces. There is nothing in the wording of the resolution itself to which anybody could take strong exception. If all were as smooth and well in the field of dominion-provincial relations as the resolution seems to make it appear then we could pass the resolution quickly, take care of the bill very quickly and get off home for at least a token summer holiday.
Unfortunately the resolution itself is misleading, and when we get into a careful study of the government's proposals to the provinces, proposals which will be embodied in detail in the bill to follow the resolution, we find that all is not well. There is widespread dissatisfaction amongst the provinces of this country. When we consider the details of the government's proposition in' the light of all the circumstances and conditions we find them most unrealistic, and practically every province looks upon them in the same way.
That would be serious enough but there is much more to make the provinces very unhappy about the whole situation. The provinces think that the federal government is trying to ram a new formula for taxation and revenue division down their throats without taking the time and making the effort to work out in conference with them a formula which will be acceptable and much more realistic in its concept. I have talked
16, 1956	6005
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements to quite a number of people from the provinces, and without a single exception that is the attitude which they have all had.
Many of the provinces believed that when the federal government called them together something over a year ago, I believe a year ago last April, to consider extension of the tax rental agreements or some suitable alternative, as well as other important matters, the conferences would continue in intermittent session until a satisfactory settlement of the most important of the financial and taxation problems outstanding between the provinces and the federal government had been worked out and agreed to. I think they are entitled to this belief. There was nothing to indicate, when they were first called together over a year ago, that they would be called together, that they would draw up an agenda for a later conference, that the conference would take place and that at that conference a proposition would be put before them and then they would be dismissed to consider whether or not they would accept it. I think, as I said, that they were entitled to believe that they would be called together and perhaps would meet intermittently until an agreement had been reached amongst them.
However, as I say, they have been sorely disappointed. Instead of continuing in conference the federal government peremptorily put a proposition before the provinces and as much as said to them, "take it or leave it". I agree with the Leader of the Opposition when he said this morning that the way the provinces look upon this thing is that it is a take it or leave it proposition. They have had no alternative. This government has declared time and again, especially at election time, that they are promoters of unity and architects of smoothly working, successful federal union. But, Mr. Chairman, their attitude as expressed in the proposals they made to the dominion-provincial conference of October last, and in what they are obviously trying to do by asking us now to pass this measure at this time, cannot be considered as promoting unity or building a nation of happy, co-operative provinces.
The provincial governments almost 100 per cent consider that this measure is a breach of faith, and so some of them have told me. I believe I am correct in saying that they consider the "take it or leave it" attitude of the government is not the basis for a smoothly working confederation. As a matter of fact, persisting in the attitude adopted by the government today will not only wreck confederation but will make for serious disunity and, what is most serious, will result in a most objectionable measure of centralization of power and authority far removed from the
6006	HOUSE OF
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements individual citizen in this country, a centralization that is completely foreign to what the fathers of confederation had in mind. To pursue this whole matter of settlement of tax fields and revenue sources as it is now being pursued by this government can, in the minds of the provinces and their governments, result in tearing up the British North America Act.
I said that the government's proposition is unrealistic and niggardly. I am going to suggest four reasons why. Time of course will not permit me to do more in the 30 minutes I have at my disposal this afternoon, but perhaps later I will have something more to say and my colleagues will also present other reasons why they think that the whole proposition the government is making to the provinces today is unrealistic.
My first reason is this. The government's proposal fails to give anything like the weight that should be given to the burdens that are now on the provinces. It almost totally disregards the terrific strain which the demands of the next 20 years are going to place on provincial budgets, and it brushes off altogether too lightly the fact that every provincial government in Canada needs more money.
Much has been said already today about the burdens that fall upon the provincial governments. The Leader of the Opposition spoke about the crisis that looms in education. I agree with him. The crisis is now on us and it is going to intensify in the years immediately ahead. We all agree that education is a provincial responsibility. Educational costs, however, have skyrocketed during the past ten years. There has been a terrific increase in building costs, in salaries, in the cost of supplies, and the end is not yet.
Here is a specific example of the sort of thing that nearly every province is forced to deal with, and it gives substance to what the Leader of the Opposition said this morning and what I am saying now, that there is a crisis in education ahead of us. Let us take Ontario. My children are going to school in Ontario and I try to keep in touch with things as they are in this province. I am interested in education and I have tried to keep myself informed about Ontario education. I see municipalities like Ottawa telling the people in certain sections of the city that the city has to look upon them in future as second-class citizens, that they cannot allow them to have a school with a basement, a wood-working shop or an assembly hall because costs have increased to the point where they cannot tax the people any more to get such things. It is all right for the other parts of the city to have them but they cannot have them for the reasons I have suggested.


Today in Ontario the public, secondary and technical school enrolment is approximately one million boys and girls. It has taken 89 years to build up to that school population. The growth over these 89 years has been quite largely gradual and steady. But official forecasts indicate that in the next ten years there will be an increase of no less than three-quarters of a million students in the public, secondary and technical schools of this province, almost the same growth in ten years as has occurred over the last 89 years. A 75 per cent increase in ten years will put a terrible strain on an already heavily burdened provincial government and the even more harassed municipalities and school districts.
What about university education? As I understand it, there are seven universities in the province of Ontario. Ontario's seven universities now have approximately 20,000 students. By 1965 it is expected that they will have 40,000, if they can be provided for. That is what the Leader of the Opposition said this morning-if they can be provided for. But what if they cannot be provided for? Are they to be denied the advantage of a university education? Are they to be denied equality of opportunity with those who have gone before? They will be, unless we solve this problem, unless we divert it, unless we meet it in some way. I am told by competent authorities that by 1975 they expect to have fully 90,000 students in those universities in this province. That is a spectacular growth in 20 years if they can be provided for.
Are the provinces to be left to pay the huge costs of meeting this situation? It is not just a question of more students; it is a question of more accommodation, more teachers, more instructors, more administrative staff. Are they to be left alone to carry on? Let us not forget that Canada has been running behind in the output of the specialist class of students which was mentioned this morning by the Leader of the Opposition, specialists in engineering, mathematics and all that sort of thing. Yet we are told that Russia and the communist countries are going ahead rapidly. Are we going to turn over this big job of providing a national bank of ability and technical skills for the development of this country and to meet the demands of the future in war and in peace to the slender resources of the provinces and the municipalities which are already over-burdened.
I could speak about British Columbia and the situation there as I talked about Ontario. In British Columbia the enrolment in the secondary and technical schools in 1954-55 was 220,000; competent authorities indicate that in 1964-65 it will be 340,000, an increase of 50 per cent in ten years; in 1974-75

it is estimated it will be 420,000. In the one university in that province which is a provincial institution it is expected that the requests for enrolment will increase from 6,300 as they were in 1955 to 26,000 in 1975. How are they to meet that situation unless they are guaranteed some sort of assurance that their revenues will be adequate to meet their responsibilities?
I could talk about a good many other things such as polluted waters and the necessity of cleaning up that situation. It is going to cost this province $120 million per year over the next 15 or 20 years and there will be no hope for any return except the satisfaction that comes from having waters which are clean. How are they to do it? I could go into a lot of these things but I must hurry on.
My second reason for saying that the present proposition is unrealistic is that it does not take into account the great upsurge in national revenues which will result very largely from the work and efforts and planning of the provincial and municipal governments. My hon. friend, the leader of the CCF, if I remember correctly has said that the wealth of Canada is produced nationally. That is pure silliness. The wealth of Canada is produced by individuals, largely as a consequence of work done by the municipalities and the provinces. While it is true that there must be some fiscal need arrangement to help the provinces with the least to get along and have something like equality, I still cannot agree that the wealth of Canada is produced nationally. The money is produced nationally, no question about that, and often times in such meagre quantities that we cannot distribute what we produce.
When one considers the very considerable growth in the gross national product and the change in the industrial activity since 1937-38 he cannot help but be greatly impressed. I think I am correct in saying that back in 1937 the gross national product of Canada was only $3-5 billion; in 1955 it reached the very marvellous figure of $26,600 million, and it is expected to reach $28 billion this year. Does the Minister of Finance think it is going to stop there? Everybody knows that it will not with the development that will take place and we know can and will take place. I am sure that he realizes that revenues will pour in to this government very largely as a consequence of the work done in the provinces and the municipalities, carried on by individuals and individual enterprise. The provinces and the municipalities ought to feel that they are getting a fair share out of those revenues in order to help pay their costs.

These things are not reflected in the proposition made by the government to the provinces. I think we should all bear in mind that it is not next year or the next five years that we should be planning for; we have to look ahead at least 20 or 30 years and plan for them. We are on the verge of a spectacular development and the provinces must have pretty definite knowledge of what they can count on by way of revenues if they are to achieve anything like what they so much desire to do and what is expected of them. The government's proposal to the provinces is most inadequate.
The third reason why I say that the present proposition put before the provinces by the government is unrealistic is that it gives no consideration whatsoever to the almost maddening frustration presently felt by the municipalities of Canada because they are faced with rapidly rising costs, increasing demands for service, but have no more money to meet them unless they carry their present property taxation to the point of confiscation, at which point I claim it is at the present time. They in turn have to look to the provinces for relief and help.
Let us not overlook the fact that in the development of this country the dominion government must always keep in mind that its strong right arm is the provinces and municipalities. Are they going to cut off that strong right arm? I could deal at some length with that but I am going to leave it for the moment.
The fourth reason I say that this proposition is unrealistic is that the governments of the provinces rightly believe that they are as much entitled to the fields of taxation as is the dominion. I do not need to enlarge upon that. Let me just say that what we have before us is a niggardly settlement of tax fields that belong as much to the provinces as to the dominion. I say it is unrealistic to take any other point of view.
During the second world war the municipalities and the provinces were strictly secondary. They had to be so. We all realized that if Canada was to make an all-out effort that must be so. The provinces willingly vacated the three tax fields on the understanding that they would be returned to them one year after the war ended. I happen to have been a signatory of the first one in 1941 and I know that the federal government told us that they would be returned at the end of the war or one year later. That was not done. This government feared that when the war was over a depression might come with peace and therefore they continued the wartime arrangements.

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements
Then war threatened again when North Korea invaded South Korea. Again it seemed necessary for security reasons for the provinces and municipalities to continue in a secondary position. Six more years have passed, years of cold war and the threat of a shooting war. It has now been sixteen years since the first tax transfer agreements were asked for by the government of Canada and during those years the senior government has come to look upon the provinces and municipalities as permanently poor relations of a second degree character.
It is easy to fall into the habit of thinking that centralization of power and authority for security purposes ought to be continued indefinitely and made a permanent arrangement. We believe that the time has come for a change of attitude on the part of the government. We face in this country an era of marvellous development. This development cannot possibly take place in the interests of all the Canadian people unless this government sets out on a deliberate and definite policy of close partnership with the provinces. You can never encourage close partnership by slapping 10 provincial premiers in the face or offending provincial governments; that is what you are doing when you put up to them a proposition like this one and then as good as say, "Take it or leave it".
Here you are bringing in legislation to give effect to a unilateral formula-that is what it is-for tax and revenue sharing; and if the bill to follow this resolution is couched in anything like the rigid terms of Bill No. 418, then it will become a stone wall behind which this government can and doubtless will take refuge when the provinces try to obtain a fair division of the revenues which will surely be available to this government in the years ahead.
With this bill made law, I can easily imagine what kind of reception the provinces will get if they come back in an effort to negotiate a better deal. They will be told doubtless in words something like these: "Parliament enacted this law and we are powerless to change it unless and until parliament shows a disposition to amend it. Sorry; we can't depart from the formula. Better go home and try to get along on what you've got." That is the way they will be dismissed. Let me point out that this could very well become a kind of closure imposed upon the provinces themselves.
I think the minister should not proceed with this resolution at this time. He should try to allay the fears of the provinces by announcing another conference some time this fall. If it could be called for October, and
[Mr. Low.l

if this government would attend that conference with a realistic attitude and with the true spirit of understanding partnership I am confident that an agreement could be reached with all or nearly all the provinces. There would then be time to prepare the legislation and get it ready to be made law early in the next session, as early as January. If that were done the provinces would not feel as if they had suffered, and when I say "suffered" I mean not merely a slap in the face but also a bad beating from this government this year.
I warn the Minister of Finance that the provinces are not at all happy about the miserable, penurious deal under which you have handed over to them and their harassed municipalities half your unemployment responsibilities, as was done just recently. There is not one satisfied province in Canada today. I challenge the minister to name one when he replies. But if the measure envisaged by this resolution is made law, then I warn him that the dissatisfaction will turn into hostility, and I am sure that feeling is not conducive to progress and sound development in Canada as we want to see it.
I remind the minister of something else in closing. I remind him of what has happened during the past 17 years. Those are the years during which the federal Liberal government has been centralizing financial and taxation authority in Ottawa. It is true that was to meet a particular situation, and we are not complaining about that. However, 17 years ago every provincial government in Canada except one was a Liberal government. One by one those Liberal provincial governments have fallen until today only three of the smaller provinces of Canada have Liberal governments, and even they are very dissatisfied and for good reason. I noticed just a few days ago where they met in Fredericton and worked out a permanent organization to seek a better deal. They are not satisfied.
Has it occurred to my hon. friends and the Minister of Finance, for whom I repeat I have very high regard, that the people of the provinces, who are closer to their governments, have turned down the Liberals by at least 12 to one on the basis of population, largely because they felt they had to turn to opponents of the Liberals for their own protection? I should think you boys over there would take a fairly careful look at the whole situation, and when you do you will perhaps give the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister some fatherly advice, prominent in which ought to be instructions to withhold this legislation until a much more sympathetic effort has been made to find a more acceptable formula. It can be done.

You should bear in mind that a good many people, Mr. Chairman, are quite aware of the fact that since 1946 this government has piled up accumulated budgetary surpluses of more than $2 billion. This is the period during which municipalities all over Canada, and many of the provinces, have been forced to raise property taxes until they amount to sheer confiscation; and still in spite of that they have sunk into a slough of debt and interest which threatens to crush them. The people in the provinces and municipalities, I will tell you, are watching the federal finances at this time.
Moreover, they see that this year, when the federal government is trying to justify a niggardly settlement of tax fields which belong as much to the provinces as to the dominion, this government will likely pile up a huge surplus of three-quarters of a billion dollars. And when they see a good part of that surplus used in the 1957 budget as election bait, as it surely will be, they will be quite satisfied in accusing this government of callous indifference to the actual needs of the municipalities and the provinces, or lack of vision and responsibility, or both. In the light of all the facts, how can the government refuse to try to seek a less penurious, less objectionable settlement of the taxation field? The minister ought to do it.
I am going to leave it at that, Mr. Chairman, but I do feel very keenly that every effort ought to be made to work out a much more justifiable settlement than this represents, to see if we cannot get a happy, smooth working democracy in this country.

I was looking at the 1952 debate on the renewal of the tax rental agreements during that year, Mr. Chairman, and I noticed that only seven members took part at the committee stage. I am informed that I am not going to be as fortunate this time, therefore I think perhaps I should answer some of the remarks that have been made and some of the questions that have been raised up to this time. Perhaps it will be necessary to intervene on another occasion.
There seems to be an advantage to the Minister of Finance on this particular matter in that he is being criticized for completely different reasons, in fact conflicting reasons. Therefore I begin by saying that possibly under those circumstances I might be comforted in thinking I have arrived at perhaps the best solution.
We have the Leader of the Opposition, not perhaps directly but indirectly, repeating the argument he made in opposition to the tax rental agreements of the past. We have the leader of the C.C.F. party upholding the tax rental system of the past and criticizing any

We have the leader of the Social Credit party taking a position which I think may be described as somewhere between the two, except that he is opposed to the change now not on the grounds of principle but simply on the grounds of the money involved in the particular solution at which we have tried to arrive.
May I for the record repeat what I said in my budget speech in connection with this, and I point out that I made this statement this morning in a different form. On March 20, at page 2335 of Hansard, I said this:
But may I make it quite clear that not one provincial premier is on record as saying that this new tax-sharing plan is not as good as the present tax rental agreements; and I am prepared to go further and say that almost all of them have stated that the principle of the new plan is better than the present system.
From that day to this no one has questioned the validity of what I said. So I am prepared to say to the committee that while there may be, and there certainly is, a difference of opinion as to how much may be paid to a province, I take it that even in this debate except for the questions of the leader of the C.C.F. party there has not been anyone who has suggested that the system we have proposed to the provinces and which is now before the committee, is not better than the previous system.

I made the statement that no premier had said it was not as good, and I am prepared to say that most of them have said it was better. I say that because in all the meetings and in all the correspondence no premier has suggested that we should continue with the tax rental agreements as they are now in existence, even with increased payments, and they have all agreed at one time or another that this system is a better system for the purpose of distribution, if you like, of certain tax receipts among the provincial governments. Now, that is not to say that they have agreed on any detail whatever of the plan. I merely confine myself for the moment to the principle.
But may I go back and cover some of the points made by the Leader of the Opposition. I have been astonished at the repetition of what I consider a fallacy in his argument even today with respect to what happened under the wartime tax rental agreements. He has made the point, or has tried to make it, that when the federal government entered the field of taxation for wartime purposes by agreement we in some manner avoided carrying out the engagements that were made at the time so there has been a disadvantage to the provincial governments.
6010	HOUSE OF
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements I want to read what was contained in the wartime tax agreements with respect to this point. I am quoting:
The federal government undertakes-
-to reduce its rates of taxes by such an amount as will enable the province again to use the income tax and corporation tax fields, and in particular the dominion undertakes to reduce its rate of tax on corporation incomes by at least 10 per cent of such incomes.
That was the extent of the undertaking given at that time. May I point out what we have done. As from January 1, 1947, at the conclusion of those agreements, the federal tax rates were substantially reduced and the conditions met. Corporation income taxes were reduced by 10 percentage points and personal income taxes by well in excess of 20 per cent. These reductions were in excess of the levels of taxation prevailing in any province prior to the wartime tax agreements. Well, we went farther, sir. When we entered into the 1947 tax rental agreements we also agreed to certain conditions which we would meet at the termination of those agreements. We agreed to allow a deduction of provincial personal income tax up to 5 per cent of the federal tax, a deduction for provincial succession duties up to 50 per cent of the federal duties, and a deduction for corporation income tax up to one-seventh of the federal tax.
Our performance with respect to that undertaking is this. At the conclusion of the agreements these conditions were met exactly in the case of the personal income tax and succession duties, while in the case of corporation income tax a credit of 5 per cent was allowed, which was in excess of the one-seventh of the prevailing federal rate.
We have similar conditions in the 1952 tax rental agreements. We agreed at the termination of those agreements to allow a 5 per cent credit for personal income, a 50 per cent credit for succession duties and a 7 percentage points credit for corporation income tax. These conditions will be more than met with a 10 per cent personal income abatement, a 50 per cent succession duty abatement, and an allowance of 9 per cent-age points for provincial corporation taxes, as is proposed in the legislation before the committee at the moment. Therefore I am completely unable to accept the argument advanced by the Leader of the Opposition that we have failed at any time to carry out any engagement that was made, beginning with the wartime tax rental agreements.
When I interrupted the Leader of the Opposition this morning with respect to the argument he was making as to the result this would have, I gathered he had in mind that not only should we vacate those tax fields,


as we have done on successive occasions, but that we should continue the former arrangement, as he said, and I read from the Hansard typewritten sheets of his answer to my question-
Before the war there had been arrangements under which certain of the provinces were imposing taxes, and that was in the mind of those who were arranging the agreements at that time. It was understood that immediately afterwards those provinces that wished to do so would again impose taxes and that the federal government would carry out the arrangements which it carried out before the war with respect to collecting those taxes up to the amount imposed by the provinces and without double taxation. That was the simple and clear understanding at that time.
I asked at that point if this bill was not doing that and, of course, he said that in effect the bill may be doing so at the moment but that we had not done so in the past. I have examined the record, and I cannot find any undertaking whatever by the federal government to go on collecting taxes at the conclusion of the war period on the same basis as before. However, let me point out that we are offering to do it at the present time and the conclusion of the tax rental agreements.
The leader of the C.C.F. party has made a number of suggestions as to why we seem to be retreating from the position we took in 1945. He knows quite as well as I do-and I think I should repeat this although he has heard it many times-that the green book offer of that year was conditional on a great many things which were not met, including the fiscal arrangements contained in the suggestions in the green book. On the other hand, I think he can go through the green book, and while he can make arguments with respect to the price of goods to be purchased now as compared with the price at that time, he will find it somewhat difficult to pick out any offer we made at that time that has not been carried out or is not about to be carried out by offers that are now outstanding.

speechtext:
Just a moment. This is from
the green book in which those offers were made conditional upon certain other arrangements being entered into, which have not been met, and for that reason the original offer was vitiated.
I take it his argument is that the tax rental agreements now in existence have met to a considerable degree the fiscal need of some provincial governments at least; yet because they hid the fiscal need element, they were to be preferred to the present system. Let me answer that very briefly by saying this. The present system will show

quite clearly the amount whereby the taxpayers of a given province are not able to contribute in these three tax fields to the extent of other taxpayers in other provinces, and we have based the equalization payment on the deficiency between any given province and the average of the highest two provinces. In this way everyone can see at a glance what that deficiency is from year to year, and will be able to decide whether or not this parliament should make a deficiency payment in this particular case to the extent that the legislation calls for.
I would suggest to the leader of the C.C.F. party that it is far better to know the extent of the fiscal need that is being met in this matter, so that if the argument should be made that this government is not aiding in this particular field we can see what is being done; and if the argument should be made that it is not enough we have the statistics on which we can base our decision on that argument.
I noticed also that he emphasized more than once in the course of his remarks that we seem to have given up some of the authority and the power we had to control by taxation the difficulties that we may become involved in if we have another depression. Well, now, sir, we are not doing that to any great extent. It is true that to the extent that a provincial government may elect to impose and collect its own taxes under the legislation now before us there will be that diminution, if you like, in the almost complete authority of this parliament to impose taxation in those fields which has existed when all but one of the provinces have made tax rental agreements, as has been the case in the last four or five years; and yet, sir, I suggest that that slight diminution, if it is serious at all, is not by any means serious enough to take away from this parliament whatever opportunity it may have to exercise by fiscal policy, some changes in the economy from time to time. If I had thought that there would be any other result I would not have presented this resolution in its present form.
I believe-and I think the leader of the C.C.F. recognizes this-one of the principal problems in carrying on with a tax rental system such as we had is that despite the expression of opinion in 1945 that it would be desirable to maintain that authority in this parliament against the possibility of a post-war depression-and I think I should add here that I never heard of anyone who did not expect a depression at that time; everyone was apprehensive, therefore the thinking and planning of everyone was coloured a little by that-it should be borne in
16, 1956	6011
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements mind that since that time we have had only the slightest of recessions in 1954 and during that time it was quite clear that the whole of the provinces of Canada were not going to be in agreement with the tax rental system that we began at that time. That is a political fact that ought to be considered and due weight should be accorded to it.
Therefore, as I said in my introductory remarks, when we came to consider what should be done when the tax rental agreements ran out we were obliged to think of another system that would meet the needs of the people and maintain in this house to a large extent the power and authority for taxation purposes that have been mentioned, as well as to recognize, if we come to the other argument, that the tax rental system imposes upon provincial governments some restraint on their autonomy, a restraint which is not good in the long run. So we had to consider whether some system might be devised under which if they wished they might return to taxation in those particular fields on their own terms to a certain extent.
Briefly the Leader of the Opposition and the leader of the C.C.F. party referred to the weaknesses of the Weimar constitution, and I think I could add one to it. My recollection is that the first constitution of the United States provided for maintenance of the central government by the governments of the 13 states, and it too fell by the way for the simple reason that you cannot have a central government dependent on the support of the constituent parts of that central government. For good or ill a central government must stand on its own feet and must be able to exercise the authority and powers which it is called upon to do by the constitution. Inevitably, in a country like Canada at least, the central government when times are not as good as they are at the moment would have to stand behind the provincial governments in any crisis that might arise, as it did in the depression which brought about all the things we are talking about now.
We should not overlook the fact that while the Leader of the Opposition seemed to suppose I should have found a solution to this problem in the past few years, the history of this problem only goes back to the depression of 25 years ago, and we have experimented with only one solution, which was the tax rental system to overcome the difficulties reported on by the Rowell-Sirois commission.
It is true the provinces accepted the tax rental system during the war simply on an emergency basis; the Leader of the Opposition is quite right in saying that. On the
6012	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements other hand it is equally certain that a great many people in Canada would have desired that the Rowell-Sirois commission report be carried out before the war in one form or another, and that when the war ended there were a great many people who felt that the advantages of the single tax system in these particular fields should be maintained, that at any rate the advantages to certain provinces and communities by reason of distribution of these tax fields had been very great and should not be discontinued.
That has been the policy of this party. We have upheld the tax rental system in two general elections, as the leader of the C.C.F. party mentioned. We have been upheld in those general elections not because of the tax rental system itself but because the result of it was that we were able to provide the provincial governments with extra revenue they could not get by their own means, and in that manner they were able to provide services for their people which otherwise would not have been provided.
The leader of the C.C.F. party remarked that we might possibly be losing our powers to control unemployment. We have, of course, provided a means of alleviating the difficulties that arise with unemployment, but I suggest that the record of this government in maintaining a high level of employment over the past 10 years at least has been such that no criticism can be directed at it at the moment. We are today approaching a time when there will be a shortage of labour in Canada, and practically everyone who can work will be working. Indeed I think we have passed that point until now people are saying, "Let us have more hands." Everyone is working.
I do agree with one thing that is said with respect to succession duties. There is no question at all, sir, that this duty is one which in my opinion should be collected by the federal government and by provincial governments if they so desire, of course. It is true that the facilities for becoming wealthy in Canada are not confined to any municipal corporation or any provincial area, and that when great wealth is made it is usually made throughout the dominion. In my view in this particular instance it would be desirable to maintain the collection of succession duties for the purpose mentioned by the leader of the C.C.F. party.
A great deal has been said about the ill effects of double taxation. There is no question about it that double taxation is undesirable in Canada from a practical standpoint and from the standpoint of the taxpayer. He would prefer to make one return and deal with one government so that his

costs could be kept down and so on. On the other hand it should not be overlooked that we in this country have a federal system with provincial governments, and one should not expect to take away from them the right of taxation if they desire to do so, except by their own consent.
I must say the fact that some provincial government might choose to impose taxes in these fields rather than agree to a tax rental system does not bother me particularly because I realize that while there will be in that particular province a little bit of difficulty for the taxpayer in filling out more taxation forms and satisfying a second government instead of only one, I think this will be accepted by the taxpayer in that province on the basis that the provincial government in its wisdom feels it is desirable to enter this field either for maintaining its autonomy or for the purpose of obtaining a greater revenue from the particular tax than that which we would be able to provide by the tax rental agreement.
The leader of the Social Credit party has perhaps given greater condemnation than any others of the offer we have made. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, I am not in a position to say that under some conditions we could not have provided a greater percentage in the standard rates than we have at the present time. All I can say is that we met in conferences, and may I say at this point that they were conferences. There was discussion, and there was no take it or leave it attitude. Although I was not a member of any other conference I have spoken to many who were members of previous conferences, and I have been told by them that these several conferences were conducted in a better spirit than any others have been, which is an indication that we were not adopting a take it or leave it attitude.
I pointed out at the conference last year that I thought perhaps I was the only minister of finance or provincial treasurer present who would show a deficit during the last fiscal year. My recollection is that one of them mildly disagreed with me on the ground that in his province there was apt to be a deficit under certain conditions. I think the committee should bear in mind that we did have a deficit in our fiscal matters in the last fiscal year. It is true that this year we expect to have a surplus as I indicated in March and that surplus is due, as everyone knows, to the increased activity in the country together with the delayed effect of the payment of corporation income taxes.
This, of course, does not redound to our complete advantage under the system we have here. As corporation and individual

income taxes and succession duties increase, the provincial governments will receive the appropriate increase that we have provided in the legislation. We are not tying them down for five years to the maximum amount they are going to receive next year so that from then on they are constant while we take the extra payment; by no means. They are getting their share of the increased payment if there is an increased payment of tax in these fields.
On the other hand, and this should not be overlooked, we are guaranteeing the provincial governments that they shall not fall below a certain level, no matter what those payments may amount to. That guarantee is a very essential and very desirable part of those arrangements from the standpoint of the provincial governments. It might happen that we shall not have to use the guarantees we have given. As I said this morning, we should hope that conditions in the country would be such that it would not be necessary, but I think we have to accept the fact that as difficulties arise this government must see that on all occasions the revenues of the provincial governments do not fall materially or drastically because of conditions arising throughout the country as a whole.
The leader of the Social Credit party has called these proposals niggardly. I have been finding it difficult to understand this language, sir, because the document I tabled this morning indicates that if the tax rental agreements have been good from the standpoint of payment-and no one particularly has said they were not reasonably good-surely this is better, when every province receives at least as much under the proposals before the committee, and in most cases more than they would under the tax rental agreement if it were extended into the following year. I do not know what one would consider an adequate increase in provincial revenues from year to year might be, but let me point out that this means a 20 per cent increase in the payment from this government to the provincial governments. Further than that, the amount being paid comes, I think, to an average increase in provincial budgets across the country of about 8 per cent, and in some cases more than that. It seems to me, whilst I would not be in a position to judge whether any provincial government would feel that it ought to have more than that, if you find an average of 8 per cent it would mean that some had around 11 or 12 per cent. That is a fairly substantial increase in gross revenues in any year, and provincial governments probably would not be in any particular financial strait-jacket, as has been suggested during this debate.

Now I want to point out one other thing. The Leader of the Opposition made some fun over my remark about not having a solution to this problem. I said a moment ago that we have been only experimenting with it for less than 20 years. We have only had a report suggesting something like this for less than 20 years. I should not suggest that we could arrive at a final and conclusive solution at this time. We have followed only one system up to the present time, tax rental agreements negotiated separately with the provincial governments. We are now attempting here a solution which is not final-that is why I did not use the word-and which even the Leader of the Opposition described as having merit.
In fact I suggest now that it has this merit, that when the terms have become known it will be seen that about the only argument that might be made against it is with respect to the amount of money involved under any given circumstances, and that the need of the provinces is clearly set out. The federal government makes certain payments under certain conditions; and for these reasons the provincial premiers who studied it, whilst dissatisfied no doubt with respect to the amount of money involved, have not, as I have said, suggested to us that any other system would be better than the one we have suggested here.
When the bill is before the house, of course, I shall go into much greater detail than I have done today; but 1 suggest that if any increase in contributions to the provinces to the extent of 8 to 12 per cent is going to be described as niggardly, then 1 am afraid I shall not be able to carry on a discussion on that basis. I suggest that it is a good increase, one which may not perhaps be acceptable in some quarters, but which does not tie down the provinces over a period of 20 years, as has been stated here today.
I realize that the provincial governments, like this government, cannot plan just from year to year, though we only tax from year to year. We must be aware of the problems that are going to arise from time to time, but this government engages upon programs which are not completed in one year. We have programs going on which we know will not be completed for another three or four years. We have embarked upon them with what money we get from year to year in the meantime to complete them. Therefore we limited the proposal before the committee to five years.
I for one would doubt that in five years' time the system would remain precisely what it was. At that time, as I said this morning, there will perhaps be different
6014	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements men dealing with this matter, with different ideas as to whai ought to be done, but this plan is good for five years. I do not think it is going to destroy the municipalities and provincial governments in the meantime. What is more, I think it is going to be advantageous to them. At that time, if a change is required perhaps it may be worked out. In the meantime I suggest that we ought to rely on the opinion I have given, namely that so far no one has suggested a better system, and we can discuss it in detail when we come to the bill.

speechtext:
I am not going to get involved in a discussion with the Minister of Finance as to what may or may not have been suggested or what may or may not have been done in years gone by. The Leader of the Opposition and others who have participated in this debate will have an opportunity of speaking again at other stages, and I am sure the record will be dealt with effectively at that time.
The minister has given us a fairly long dissertation upon his philosophy and the philosophy which he thinks motivates those who have proposed this resolution. I cannot disagree with him in everything. As the Leader of the Opposition said this morning, there are good points about this legislation. As was said, opinions may differ as to whether this is scientific surgery or sophisticated butchery.
We saw a difference here this afternoon among the leader of the C.C.F. party and the leader of the Social Credit party and the Leader of the Opposition. Like the three blind men dealing with the elephant in the dark, one felt the leg and one felt the side, one felt the trunk, and they each got a different reaction. So it is not something on which one can be dogmatic in every respect. There have to be qualifications in anything which may be said. However, I would take some objection to what the Minister of Finance said to the effect that the support which his party got in elections in the past had been partly attributable to the fact that people in some provinces realized they were getting moneys as a result of those tax rental agreements which otherwise they would not have got. Actually I do not think that can be justified at all, because those agreements, as the Minister of Finance knows full well, were not designed for the purpose of distributing the wealth in any way. As a matter of practice, in the end federal agreements were made with the wealthier provinces which were much more lucrative than those made with the provinces which had less, and which were compelled to sign because if they did not sign they would

starve to death. It had nothing whatsoever to do with the distribution of the means of this country in any shape or form.
If one reads the history of this, one sees how complicated it is. The minister made reference to the Rowell-Sirois report and the studies carried on before the war.
There is no question but that at that time it was envisaged by that commission that there should be a centralization of taxation, a recasting of federal responsibilities and duties under confederation. Many things were envisaged then including, of course, the fact that taxation was necessary as a fiscal instrument in order to control or deal with depressions. That is one factor the member for Rosetown-Biggar referred to this afternoon, and I think the Minister of Finance suggested it. I believe he will admit that today the emphasis is placed on central banking and on monetary policy, and that the government realize that perhaps in that field they have a more effective weapon to deal with depressions should they come, so they are not so dependent upon taxation and therefore have been willing to relax some of the powers of taxation which they previously controlled.
There are many criticisms one could level. I propose to deal only with two this afternoon and to do so briefly, because the ground has been covered in general by other speakers and there will be others speaking as well who will perhaps develop the other points. The Minister of Finance says, "Oh, there have been conferences, and it is unfair to suggest that there have not been conferences." Well, you can call them conferences, Mr. Chairman. We have also had consideration in this house which lasted 15 seconds. That was deemed consideration. We have the minutes here of the conferences, and we can see what voluminous documents they are. They certainly are conferences only by courtesy. They made long speeches. In fact they took all one day complimenting each other all around the table, and then wont onto camera on the second day. But surely no one is going to suggest, least of all the Minister of Finance who understands the complicated constitutional problem with which this country is confronted, that in such a short time as was taken by these conferences one could attempt to deal with the various problems confronting the governments of Canada today.
The minister says, "Oh, my, we have only spent 25 years considering this and we have made remarkable progress because we have got away from the leasing type of taxation agreement and now, after 25 years, we are going to try something else which is a step

beyond that, and only a step, and which is only going to tie our hands for five more years." He admits, and quite wisely I think, that after 30 years there may be somebody else there who will be able to deal with this matter in some other way. Yet during that 25 years the constitutional problem in this country has only been brought particularly into crisis since the war.
Certainly there was no great need of haste, no great need of immediate decision in the horse and buggy day, in the red school house day, even in the days not too long prior to the second world war. But the pressure which has been brought to bear on the provinces and municipalities by circumstances over which they had no control at all necessitates and requires that some decision be arrived at on the over-all picture rather than a piecemeal attempt to deal with it by this so-called conference when, as a matter of fact, the premiers of the provinces were called together and told, "Here is our proposition; now, take it or leave it."
That is essentially the situation. This time they were given an escape clause if they did not want to take it. They were given a part of the back yard in which to play. It was not fenced off but they were told, "If you do not want to accept this, then you can go and play in the back yard. We will give you a little part of it where you can exercise your own taxation powers." In other words we have a feudal complex which arose first out of wartime pressure, and having made use of the last agreements for their own ends the government now feel that they should have the right to control these moneys collected by the central taxing authority, whatever the effect may be on the provinces and municipalities.
We in this party believe and have said time and time again that there should be a reallocation of responsibilities, that there should be a reallocation of taxation powers, and that this should be done by a constitutional conference properly called where these matters could be given consideration, where time could be given to them, and where the problems of Canada in the last half of the twentieth century could be faced. One of our objections to this type of agreement is that it fails to recognize that problem. The government says to the provinces, "We are being a little bit more generous. However, you do not have to lease. If you do not want to, you will be given a little bit of space in the back yard in which to play, but we are going to continue to exercise control over the collection of revenues and how we shall spend them."
What did the Minister of Finance say this morning? I made a note, and I think I took
16, 1956	6015
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements him down correctly. After dealing with the responsibilities of the provinces he said, "In our view"-there is the feudal right, the seigneur surveying the field-"this proposal will give the provinces the revenues necessary to meet their needs in so far as possible." He said, "in our view". There we have the view of the government of Canada determining what revenues are going to be necessary for the provinces and determining that in so far as possible, whoever may control that possibility-

That had regard to the matters envisaged by this resolution and the control of the taxation fields. Then the minister went on to say all the things that Canada was doing for the provinces. He listed them and suggested that they ran into several hundred million dollars. That is true, Mr. Chairman. There are many things being taken over by the dominion, some of them I think necessarily so, and many more that perhaps should be taken over. But our objection is that they are being taken over indirectly. The government is coming in through the back door and doing something which should be done through the front door, and should be arranged definitely and fairly and on a basis on which agreement can be reached between the provinces and the dominion.
Frankly, some of us get rather tired of being told at election time that so and so, Paul somebody, is giving the people the baby bonus or is giving increased old age pensions, as if the government were reaching down into its own pocket for the money and giving it to the people out of generosity, when as a matter of fact the money is provided by taxes collected in fields which, at one time at least, were constitutionally believed to belong to the provinces at least as much as, if not more so, than the dominion.
So the time has come, as the Leader of the Opposition and others have emphasized today, with the increased problems confronting the municipalities and the provinces, to deal with this matter on a more constructive basis. Surely the time has now come after 25 years-and we admit that part of that time was a period of war with all the stresses, strains and difficulties of war; no one will question that for a moment-when these matters can be dealt with on a more constructive basis, a long term program worked out and the problem dealt with in such a way that the responsibilities of the municipalities and the provinces, which are suffering from an impossible burden of taxation, which are called upon to perform services in the field of education, the field of highways, the field
6016	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements of public health, for which they have not the money, may be met now and dealt with on a long term and permanent basis.
It is true, as the minister says, that the dominion has heavy taxation and financial burdens. We realize that; but it is quite possible and I hope and think more than likely, that within the next year, two years or three years that lie ahead the heavy burden resting upon the dominion will lighten substantially because of improvement in the international situation, reconsideration of defence expenditures and the rest of it. The burdens resting on the provinces and the municipalities certainly cannot lighten in any way. They are going to increase. Their revenues are frozen until they are given reconsideration and until the whole situation is dealt with properly and, after conference, they are relieved of some of the responsibilities, with the federal government taking them over in a proper way rather than doing it indirectly, casually and in a haphazard and piecemeal way as has been done heretofore.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said a while ago that the federal government needed these increased revenues so it could deal with the requirements of the provinces and the municipalities. He intimated that he hesitated to advocate anything being done which would result in a reduction of income to the dominion. I think it has been pointed out today that there is little probability of a reduction of income to the national treasury. If this expansion goes on, and we know it will go on, over the long-term period-there may be minor areas of recession-with our natural resources there is bound to be an increase in the national wealth of this country.
There need be little worry about the dominion finding itself in a strait-jacket in dealing with the problem. As a matter of fact it has been pointed out by the Leader of the Opposition that the probability is that we will have a surplus of $500 million or $750 million or some such astronomical figure at the end of this fiscal year. Yet what happened? The provinces are given a little largess, a little gesture of help, and then the Minister of Finance says "In our opinion that is enough for you to carry out your provincial responsibilities".

There certainly is something wrong with the principle suggested by this government in this resolution. Again it is based on a per capita formula. A rather involved formula is proposed whereby you take the average of British Columbia and Ontario and apply that on a per capita basis, and the provinces below that average are to be reimbursed on that basis. That does not take into consideration at all the ability to pay as well as the population itself.
If you want to see the results of the application of the per capita basis just look at the payments made to the universities. The universities in the maritimes receive, as I pointed out the other day, in one case only $80 per student, while a university in another province receives over $400. If the Minister of Finance wants an argument with respect to that I can give him one which he certainly cannot accuse of being partisan. I would refer him to the argument advanced by the premier of Nova Scotia at the conference in April. At that time the premier took violent objection to the proposal that this should be worked out on a per capita basis.
I am not going to quote his words, but he went on to say that you could have a province with a per capita income of $900 and you could have another province where

the income was $1,200, and then you could work out something on a per capita basis, but the fact remained that the people in the provinces having only $900 of income would have very little left after paying their federal taxes with which to pay their provincial taxes, whereas in the other province, though they might feel that they were being overtaxed and undoubtedly could claim an increased burden of taxation, nevertheless they would have greater means with which to pay the provincial taxes to meet the provincial requirements. In the case of the poorer provinces they would not be able to do that and would have to rely almost entirely on the per capita grant. The province which fell below the average would be given something. But a formula should be worked out that would recognize the capacity to pay of the individual as well as the number of heads in a province. That the government has not done.
The maritime provinces submitted formulas to the conference under which they sought equitable treatment. One province approached [DOT] the problem in one way and worked out a mathematical formula which could be justified. Another province decided what they needed in order to carry on their services, and they translated that into a formula. They both arrived at virtually the same formula. I am not going to try to check those formulas now because the minister knows very well that they were presented to the conference. But with what result? In this letter of January 14, 1956, to the premier the Prime Minister said this:
At the same time we made it clear that the present government had no intention of abandoning the objective of the tax rental agreements which is to make it financially possible for all the provinces whatever their tax base to perform their constitutional functions themselves and to provide a reasonable Canadian level of provincial services without an abnormal burden of taxation. That is the foundation of the policy of the federal government.
If that is the foundation I certainly say they failed to build on that foundation. The premiers of the Atlantic provinces made it abundantly plain that the foundation is most unstable. It reminds me of what was said about the man who built his house on the sand. The rains fell and the winds blew, his house fell, and great was the fall thereof. This is a sand foundation which you are constructing under the financial structure of Canada. We must have something that will provide a more stable fabric on which this country can be built, something which will provide rock and not sand.
What the end will be it is difficult to say, but it is not one which is going to add to the standard of government of the

The present proposal in essence does not approach this objective-
That is the objective I just read.

It did, pretty well.

Our government is now asked to accept a situation which does practically nothing to relieve the special disabilities under which we have laboured for so long. The formula which we presented to the conference envisaged transfer payments to our treasury of some ten millions of dollars more than we were receiving annually under the 1952 tax agreements. This amount is based on a realistic appraisal of our minimum requirements, if we are to be able to carry out our constitutional responsibilities. The proposal of your government would increase payments to New Brunswick by about $1 million annually, 10 per cent of our indicated requirements.
This small percentage of the $10 million special adjustment grants envisaged by our formula will not enable us to provide the health and social needs, the educational facilities and services, the public works, the material benefits and cultural advantages-all of which are the birthright of an industrious and enlightened people.

That is the statement of the premier of New Brunswick with respect to these tax agreements. Now, we are told that this is a solution of the problems of the have-not provinces. It is no such thing. It is only a palliative. It makes no approach to an actual solution of the problems at all. New Brunswick requested $10 million, and actually Nova Scotia and New Brunswick were within a few dollars of each other as to what was required by each province in order to put them on a basis where they could satisfactorily perform the services required of provincial governments in this country today. They were refused and told that 10 per cent of that was the amount to which they would be entitled. I do say, Mr. Chairman, that is not the way to deal with the legitimate demands of the provinces.
When the Minister of Finance tries to stand up, smile and shrug his shoulders and say, "I did not hear anyone say they were dissatisfied with it", or something to that effect; "I did not hear anyone suggest anything better"; he knows that many of the provinces are in a position where they have to accept this whether they like it or not.
It is true it is an improvement over the days when people were allowed to starve. You are allowed now to eke out an existence because of the largess of this government which has pre-empted to itself this whole lush area of taxation, which undoubtedly it should occupy to a greater extent than it did in the earlier days, I grant you; but let us see that the moneys are divided properly. Let us see in particular that we have no more thoughts about this being for the benefit of the have-not provinces, as the minister told us, provided for them at the expense of the haves, because that is simply a fairy story and has no relation whatever to reality.
For these two reasons and others, I propose to vote against this resolution when the times comes.

I feel it is my duty to say a few words on these agreements, Mr. Chairman. Having had something to do with many agreements, may I say that I do not ever expect the time to arrive in this world when two parties will get together where money is involved and come away with a satisfactory agreement. There is going to be something wrong with it. If there were not the two people would not be human. At least I have never seen one that was completely satisfactory to all concerned.
I have always supported the dominion-provincial agreements, because I remember back to 1939. I think the measure of the agreements, if you are going to be realistic about it, can be seen if you ask yourself the
[Mr. Nowlan.l

question whether you are better off with the agreements or without them. I can answer that in the affirmative so far as Nova Scotia is concerned. I do not want to go back to 1939. This province under the present taxing agreement is much better off than it would be if there were no agreement.
I think the main principle behind the dominion-provincial agreements, and the main reason I support them, is that in a country like Canada where you have a huge centralization of the wealth-producing organizations in two provinces, following the pattern in the United States, the only way you will get a redistribution of wealth to the other provinces under the present mechanics of society is through these agreements.
While I am on that point I might add that so far as I am concerned I did not come into this house to fight a party, either Liberal or Conservative. When I joined the group I joined, my quarrel was with the order of society under which I grew up through the thirties into 1939 and another war.	My
quarrel was not with the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister or the Leader of the * Opposition.	My quarrel was with the
mechanics of society which left people in the circumstances in which they were previous to 1939. I see in these dominion-provincial agreements, as in the other social security measures for which the present government is legislating, at least a move in the direction of changing things from the way they were and bringing about at least some degree of equalization and sharing the wealth.
This morning the Leader of the Opposition was emphatic in saying he did not agree with the centralization of finances and the centralization of taxing powers in the hands of the federal government. He believed that decentralization was necessary. I agree that decentralization is necessary in this country, not only in the field of finance but in the field of industry. Decentralization of industry is a very important point.
While there has been a lot said by the hon. member for Peace River and others in this debate on the question of financing education in the provinces, I think the main reason for that problem is that there are a great many municipal difficulties. Premier Frost made it quite clear at the conference of mayors. He said the development had taken place so fast in this province it had created municipal difficulties with which they were not going to be able to contend, such as more schools, more sewers and streets. He suggested at that time he thought the time would have to come when everybody would have to begin thinking in terms of decentralization.

As I see the proposition of the Leader of the Opposition, it is this. While there is a concentration of the wealth-producing organizations already in the two central provinces, to ask the federal government and the members of this house to go back and place the taxation powers in the hands of the provinces would mean a further concentration of wealth in the central provinces, because of the greater industrial development and the larger fields of taxation that exist in those provinces as compared with the other provinces that are not so highly industrialized. I think the proposition would mean not only a complete centralization of the industrial development of the country in those two provinces, but if the taxation powers were handed back to the provinces you would have an 80 per cent centralization of the taxes that are paid in this country in the two central provinces. Of course that would be good for them, but it would be bad for the part of the country from which I come.
I realize that there is not a province in Canada that suffers to a greater extent with respect to municipalities financing education than the province from which I come; but I do not think that going back to the system of taxation that existed prior to those agreements will help the municipalities. In fact it will hurt them in that part of the country. I read one very good survey made by the province of Saskatchewan. It was research into school financing. It came out last year and was a beautiful job of research right across the country. I have seen several other pamphlets put out by qualified people. None of those people suggest that you are going to benefit the provinces or municipalities in the field of education by reverting to the taxation system that existed before these agreements. Every one of the briefs and analyses that I have seen hark back to the same question, namely more federal aid to education.
You see, you cannot keep on demanding that the federal government do all these things and at the same time take the position that you are not going to give them the power that is necessary to weld this country together as a nation and try to bring about some equality. I took a look at our own position, and with all due respect to the letters that were read by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, I do not agree with him. Naturally, if I were on the bargaining side of the table and I was a provincial premier I would stick out for every last nickel I could get. I would do that in negotiating for any organization or for any group of people. That is the job of the negotiator. I believe more money could be used in the maritimes, but to say that this

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements particular agreement did not do something for the province of Nova Scotia is to ignore the facts. Anyone who has taken the formula, the method of applying it as related to the population of the provinces, what the agreements were previously and what they will be when this legislation comes into force, will see that it has improved considerably. In fact the amount of money that Nova Scotia will receive under the present agreement, with the equalization, indicates that Mr. Hicks did a pretty good piece of collective bargaining, though he left the bargaining table and went back to his province not satisfied. I do not think any negotiator who is looking for some money for the people whom he represents should ever be satisfied. It is bad psychology to say you are satisfied.
In going through the agreement-and I did go through it pretty thoroughly, because I did a radio broadcast on this agreement some time ago, and to do that you have to examine the situation-I found that Mr. Hicks went back to the province of Nova Scotia with an increase of 20-1 per cent for that province. I am sure any union representative in this country who goes into a meeting with a corporation and comes out of the board room and tells the membership for whom he is negotiating that he got a 20-1 per cent increase in wages tells them something that is welcome news. It would be unexpected in many sections of industry today, but that is exactly the position in Nova Scotia.
I am not looking only at the amount of money they get at this time. I am concerned with this argument from different sections of the house and different parts of the country, and largely from provinces that are able to look after themselves, that we should get back to the system that existed previously to those agreements. I refer to the arguments that these agreements were war agreements; that they were emergencies. I believe that if the war had not broken out when it did in 1939 we perhaps would have had a revolution on the North American continent. We had a million and a half young men on the streets of this country with nothing in sight for them. If you went to Toronto even in 1940 you found hundreds of young men sleeping in the basements of churches. To say that these were war agreements designed to take care of war emergencies is to ignore the facts. I believe that those agreements would have come in any event. Had there been no war the trend we are following today would have had to be followed in order to bring about some equality in this country.
I would like to warn those who are saying that the agreements have no value and that the provinces are not getting enough-no,
6020	HOUSE OF
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements they are not getting enough-that I am prepared to hang on to the principle we have established and to continue the process of collective bargaining with the federal government in order to get the amount that we do need, in time. I think it is democratic to continue to bargain with them rather than to throw away something we have now that has a great deal of value.
If tomorrow we handed over the fields of taxation to the provinces the benefit would accrue to Ontario and Quebec. To some extent British Columbia might benefit, but to some extent every other province in this country would suffer. The important thing to remember is that by cancelling these agreements and giving back the provincial fields of taxation you would dry up the field of social security. In my judgment without these agreements, without the reallocation of the wealth from the centre to the frontiers of the provinces that have not any great industrial set-up, high succession duty collections and so on, the federal government would not have the money in the treasury to make improvements in old age security pensions, family allowances and these other things which in fact are merely redistribution of wealth and of great benefit to the whole economy of this country.
It is not giving anybody anything, because the people who are getting the money are spending it on the essentials of life. That in turn creates purchasing power, and the purchasing power in turn keeps the wheels of industry moving and keeps the employees working and producing. At the present time the federal government is committed in the field of social security alone to spend some $650 million a year. That is a lot of purchasing power in the social security measures alone. In addition to that, of course, under these agreements the maritime provinces are much better off than they were. I told the committee a moment ago that Nova Scotia is 20 [DOT] 1 per cent better off in cash under this new agreement than it was under the old one.
If we continue the process of collective bargaining we may arrive at the point where we can strike a happy medium and provide equality right across the country, but I believe we should examine our criticism very carefully. I do not know what happened at the conference in Fredericton; at least, I did not get very much news out of it. About all I heard on the newscast was that they held a meeting of four provincial premiers at Fredericton. They decided to set up a permanent organization. They appointed a secretariat. Mr. Hicks said that freight rates was one of his greatest difficulties; that the freight rate
