increase would make it more difficult for all industry in Nova Scotia to market their goods in the central markets.
I did not hear anything about these agreements. The premier of Newfoundland said they were going to get all they wanted. That is a good collective bargaining attitude. The premier of Prince Edward Island said they were going after what they wanted and he thought they could get it. I did not hear what the premier of New Brunswick had to say. He convened the conference.
I hope they will stick together, because in the final analysis this particular question is not political but economic. It is a question of bread and butter for the people in the provinces these premiers represent. I am sure that each one of them realizes, if they examine their position today and their position prior to the agreements, that they are in a much better position today than previous to the establishment of these agreements. I think this is in keeping with the trend of the times. You cannot turn the clock back and you cannot look back to prewar days to try and get a picture of what you should do today, because we are living in a spanking brand new world.
I believe that in 1939, when the war broke, the other scheme as it then existed died a natural death, and when we emerged from that war we began to build a brand new world. We are mapping the world anew. We are getting propaganda and practical demonstrations from these other countries. If you look at these things in a material way alone you can get the economic side of the picture. We have no yardstick by which to measure the future, because we are prodding into the unknown.
While some people may quarrel with this idea of centralization, I think there has to be a head to the nation. There has to be some organization that has the responsibility of giving assistance, direction and guidance in the development of our resources. There has to be some authority. As in the case of a man with eight or nine children, there has to be a boss in the house. You cannot let everyone be boss and arrange their program and do what they like on their own. The father has to take the lead and assume the responsibility for establishing law and order in the home.
Canada with its ten widely scattered provinces and with people coming in from different parts of the world has to have a good central organization, and I think that is what was envisaged at confederation. I believe anyone who sits down and reads the British North America Act as I have attempted to

do realizes it was the intention of the fathers of confederation to have a central governing body. I believe that definitely was why the maritime provinces made the sacrifices they did. They realized they could not sit off in a corner by themselves and never help to build a nation. They were aware of the geographic problems they were going to have and the difficulty of marketing their products. They lost 50 of their basic industries. The first seven banks in this country were established in Nova Scotia, and that money was used to develop the markets and resources of that province. The resources were highly developed and their market was across the road.
They sacrificed all that; and although when you read the record of that period you find men like Howe and others making quite an issue of that particular position, nevertheless the people of the maritimes were prepared to go along with that and build a nation. I think you will find that in the maritime provinces today the people are more national minded than in any other section of this country. You do not have any difficulty selling the people down there on the idea of building this country as a nation.
The hon. member for Peace River said this afternoon that the wealth of the nation is produced by the people. Sure it is, but it is not produced just in one province. The gross national product is produced by the whole country working in co-operation. You will find Cape Bretoners cutting wood in British Columbia and you will find British Columbia machinery building the causeway down in Cape Breton. You will find Ontario machinery all over this country. The product of one province being sent to another and the economy of one province complementing the economy of the others is assisting to build this country as a nation. While the individual may work with his hands and produce the wealth, nevertheless he is not doing it as an individual but as a Canadian. In so doing he is trying to build the Canada of the future as a bigger and better place for his children to inherit.
As far as I am concerned, I have already put myself on record with my own people shortly after that conference took place. I knew the importance of this agreement to the part of the country I come from. I made it my business to sit down and examine the formula and work out the exact amount of money we were going to receive under this agreement, as compared with the agreement that will expire. As I said before, in cash it amounts to an increase of 20-1 per cent which the premier of Nova Scotia is going to have to play around with. I think he will realize-

Another thought I would like to leave with the committee just before I sit down is that I do not think we are going to solve all the problems of the maritimes under this agreement. I think the main problem of the maritimes is development. We have to try to get back to the position we were enjoying in 1867. With all due respect to the
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements confreres of the four provincial premiers, I hope they will do something.
The Atlantic provinces economic council has been working now for the past two years.
It has a good secretary and some of the most important and competent people in the man-times are on that council, with their main objective that of trying to bring some stability into that province. With that, coupled with measures of this kind, I think in time we are going to bring that part of the country back to its feet by developing industry that will work on the vast resources of those provinces. There is plenty of power in Nova Scotia. It is thermal power, and it is produced reasonably. I believe that any industry locating there can obtain power as cheaply as in any section of Canada. That is my information. There is a ready supply of power in the province of Nova Scotia and particularly the part I come from.
I do not envisage that anything is going to completely solve our problems in that part of the country until we get working on them ourselves and building the economic processes that will use the materials that exist in that part of the country. This, supplemented by the kind of legislation we are discussing today and coupled with the efforts of an organization like the Atlantic provinces economic council, will lead us to a solution for the problems of the maritimes.
Whilst I support these agreements for the value they have and the work they are doing, I do not envisage them as the kind of legislation that is going to solve our problems down there, because what we need is development. What I think would help Ontario is the realization that it is overdeveloped and has developed too quickly, and that its municipal problems are going to become greater and greater for the reasons stated by Mr. Frost at the mayors' conference. When they come to that realization there is a chance that some of the industry that is rushing in here because it is close to the main market and the main centres of population will be farmed out so as to bring about a better balance in the economy of the country and some protection in the event of war.
Mr. Chairman, my time is almost up, but I want to assure the house and the Minister of Finance that as far as I am concerned I am prepared to support this agreement as a step in the right direction, with the hope that the collective bargaining process in time will bring us to the point where we get something that is more satisfactory to everybody in the country.

First I should like to say that I agree with what my hon. friend


from Cape Breton South has said regarding the problems encountered by the maritime provinces, and I think he has been very fair in his reference to this legislation. We all know that the tax rental agreements were emergency agreements at the beginning of the last war. At that time they were never intended to be of a permanent character; they were for wartime only. After the war the federal government was prepared to discontinue the wartime agreements and let the provinces get back to a system they had followed previously of collecting their own revenues and spending at will.
I well remember the first conference that was held in Ottawa after I came here in 1945. At that conference there were seven of the nine provinces that felt that something along those lines should be done. Two of the provinces were opposed to it. Of course in the original tax rental agreement all the provinces were involved. The prime minister of that day stated that unless all the provinces agreed it would be impossible to work out any agreement with the federal government. I well remember that the premier of New Brunswick at that time, Hon. J. B. McNair, fought vigorously at that conference for an arrangement that he felt would be beneficial to the province of New Brunswick.
I was proud of the stand he took at that time, and I believe that it was through Hon. J. B. McNair and some others that the arrangement we had during the war was carried on afterwards. I believe they deserved a great deal of credit.
In order to determine whether or not this arrangement we are discussing at this time is generous and fair, the reasonable method to use, in my opinion! would be to decide the amount that any province might collect from the fields that are rented to the federal government and then decide whether or not the arrangement under this proposal is fair. In looking over the figures that were supplied today by the Minister of Finance, I find that the tax fields rented by the province of New Brunswick to the federal government would yield $7,375,000. When I look down the list, I discover that under the new formula the province of New Brunswick will be paid $19,320,000. As the hon. member for Cape Breton South has said, those are the facts on which one must determine whether or not the arrangement is fair. When I look at those two sets of figures I am convinced immediately that as far as the province of New Brunswick is concerned, it is fair in every way.
Surely an agreement whereby for every dollar taken out of the province in taxation nearly $3 is returned could not be looked upon as a niggardly agreement. That is what

thus relieving the federal government of that enormous responsibility. There is over $600 million involved in these agreements. I think we must all realize that is an enormous amount of money. In fact it is practically the same as our total revenue in 1939.
That is the amount we are turning back to the provinces today. Should the federal government decide that some other plan the provinces might have was a better plan, or should there be dissatisfaction with the manner in which the agreements were negotiated by the federal government and the provinces were told to collect their own revenue and spend the money as they wished, I am sure that in the province from which I come the services we now enjoy would be greatly curtailed and any thought of improving services in the future would be forgotten.
Under this arrangement, as I have stated, we are receiving nearly $3 for every $1 taken out. I believe we should all be prepared to acknowledge that fact, and at the same time be prepared to state publicly and otherwise that in the opinion of the citizens of that area the agreement is fair and just so far as they are concerned. I agree with the principle completely because, as I have said, it is just another effort to distribute the wealth of the country fairly in order that the same services may be provided for all citizens, regardless of the part of the country in which they may live.
I know it has been most helpful to the citizens of the maritime provinces, and I hope that not only will the agreements continue for this period but that the criticisms we hear from certain sections will not be sufficiently strong to convince the Minister of Finance or the government that these agreements should be discarded because the provinces, which are finding it very difficult to get along financially at this time, would be then placed in a more difficult situation.
The member for Cape Breton South has suggested that this tax rental arrangement is not a cure-all. I am sure we can all agree with that. There is no one who would be more willing to acknowledge that fact than the Minister of Finance. He has suggested today that this is a matter that has been given a lot of thought and consideration, and that in the opinion of the greater percentage of the provincial premiers and treasurers who attended the meeting this proposal was an improvement over the old agreement. I agree that it is an improvement over the old agreement, because any agreement that provides a greater amount must be an improvement. It is true that the generosity which has been extended to the maritime provinces under this agreement will be of more benefit.

The one cure-all for that part of the country is cheap power, and at the present time that is something we cannot see in prospect. I do hope the day will come when we can develop electrical energy in the Atlantic provinces at a cost comparable to that in other parts of Canada. When that time comes I can see some hope for the development of manufacturing and industry. Until we can find some way to develop electrical energy at a more reasonable cost than is possible at the present time we must carry on as we have in the past.
I believe that conditions there at this time are much better than they were 15 years ago, as the hon. member for Cape Breton South pointed out. I believe they will improve in the next 15 years. I assure the Minister of Finance that the people I represent consider that this arrangement will be helpful to the citizens of our province. I am prepared to support it, and I know in doing so it will be approved by those who receive the benefits.

Mr. Chairman, we are discussing a measure the heart of which seems rather difficult to get at. There seems to be a considerable amount of disagreement among hon. members who have spoken as to interpretation. I believe that in general most of the hon. members who have participated have forgotten that this measure is a direct descendant, shall I say, of the Rowell-Sirois commission and the Rowell-Sirois report, and also that the Rowell-Sirois report was put before the conference with the provinces on January 14, 1941, and was unconditionally rejected by three of the premiers, conditionally rejected by three, and supported by only three. It is the fact that three premiers of Canada were free enough, brave enough and patriotic enough to reject that recommendation that makes it possible for us to consider this measure today.
If we can all keep that in our minds it will help us to view this measure against a background which might considerably modify our attitude toward it. We can now ask ourselves who were behind the Rowell-Sirois report? Who were the people who caused the Rowell-Sirois commission to be set up? What was the aim of those people? Are those people aiming to accomplish the same thing today? Is this measure designed to be a move in the direction of the achievement of the objectives which the movers behind the Rowell-Sirois commission and the Rowell-Sirois report had in mind years ago?
The danger we face is that the same men who designed the Rowell-Sirois commission
16, 1956	6025
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements and the Rowell-Sirois report may be in position today to influence very forcibly the present government, this Liberal government which is the successor of the government of William Lyon Mackenzie King, who I believe against his will set up the Rowell-Sirois commission and who I believe against his will called the provinces together in January, 1941 and asked them to decide in war-time on a matter which threatened the peace and harmony and unity of this nation.
There will be some who will say that is pretty extreme. Maybe it is, but I am afraid it is not. Everywhere we look today we see restless pressure for centralization. They are not content to allow people to govern themselves. We are working in NATO to deprive people of their sovereignty as nations, in organizations like the United Nations to deprive them of their sovereignty as nations. We have already accepted Bret-ton Woods with the object of depriving nations of their sovereignty. We are talking of world government to accomplish the same objective. It is everywhere in the air and everywhere in the press if we just listen and look. Can we expect that the men who are fundamentally and signally behind this centralization movement may not be seeking for centralization in Canada which could destroy the British North America Act?
When Major C. H. Douglas, the founder of Social Credit, was in Alberta in 1934 he told us that the two most perfect constitutions in the world were the British North America Act and the constitution of Australia. He told us that the powers who were seeking for centralization in the world were seeking by every means at their command to destroy those constitutions. Until they can destroy the British North America Act the sovereignty of the provinces cannot be destroyed. It will not matter very much if they get complete control of the central government of Canada because the provinces can denounce the decisions which that central government may make.	J
I think a fairly good case can be made out for the general proposition that there is danger in this measure on the very score that it is a measure designed to weaken the British North America Act. One thing about it that leads one to suspect that is the fact that for the first time, as I recall, the bill has been sought to be introduced as a sort of enabling legislation. The bill had been planned to be introduced before the provincial premiers were called together in conference to make a decision. As I recall it that is so, if I am not right, then bring along the evidence. I do not have all the information, but I have quite a little bit respecting these matters.

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements In this case the provincial premiers did not meet and agree with the federal government as to the details which would be embodied in the act which will follow this resolution. The resolution is worded, apparently, to make it so that, as the hon. member for Peace River pointed out, the decision will in large measure already have been made before the provincial premiers come together in a conference. At least there will be a law on the statute books of Canada which can be used as a means of exerting most severe pressure on the provinces which, under the circumstances of tension, a measure of confusion and haste and all that kind of thing, can be used to cause a number of the provinces to weaken in their stern resolution to resist any encroachment upon the fundamental rights of the provinces to provincial autonomy. There is the great danger as I see it, and that is the great danger that more than one premier sees in this measure.
Now, if this kind of procedure is adopted at this time, then five years from today, using this as a precedent, another measure could be adopted just a little more severe. The first thing we know in perhaps 15 years we shall have the provinces in a position where everything will be almost cut and dried before they get together to discuss the arrangements to be made.
While mine is going to be probably more or less a philosophical approach to the whole matter, I suggest that some of the evidence which I feel I can adduce before the house will be most interesting to a great many members as evidence upon which they can base their thinking.
I think there is no doubt that it is agreed that after the premiers rejected the recommendations of the Rowell-Sirois commission in January, 1941, and the dominion came back to them with the proposition that they would have a tax transfer agreement, in connection with which there was a certain amount of financial reward to the provinces. It is agreed that the end result financially to the provinces of the tax transfer agreement was beneficial. It is agreed by everyone that, when we came to the next two agreements, which were tax rental agreements, the net result was beneficial to every province, I think, probably, even to Ontario and Quebec, though I am not in a position to judge very well in respect of those two provinces. Certainly there was a substantial amount of financial advantage to provinces like Alberta, British Columbia and the maritimes. As a matter of fact every province in the dominion benefited, except perhaps Ontario and Quebec; they might have lost.

Now, in this resolution, we come to a third type of agreement. We had first the tax transfer; then we had the tax rental agreements twice, and now we come to another kind of agreement, apparently. The name of it is given here in the last part of the resolution as "tax collection agreements". I believe it is sound for each of the provinces as a whole to say, in effect, to the dominion government -Alberta, for example, might say this. "We as a province do not possess the necessary power to tax the Canadian Pacific, for instance, and make them pay. We have not the power to tax many other corporations". Most provinces would say almost exactly the same thing. Now the dominion government has full power to tax these corporations and make them pay their share of taxation toward the financial well-being of this country. Alberta, therefore, would say to the dominion, and the other provinces along with Alberta would say the same thing, "You tax them, and then divide the money up between us and yourself". This would be sound so long as the province of Alberta took the initiative, and the other provinces likewise took the initiative.
When, however, we get to a point where the central government says, "We are going to tax all these corporations and we are going to give you, the provinces, what we think you ought to get according to a formula," then that is approaching the problem from exactly the opposite to the right method. The first approach, where the provinces take the initiative and agree as to what should be done, is the democratic method. It is the method which you would expect to be used in a federal state where each of the members is a sovereign province under the queen.
That, constitutionally speaking, is exactly the state of affairs here in Canada now, and that is exactly the state of affairs I believe I want to hand down to my children, that the provinces be sovereign just as the fathers of confederation made them. If the dominion government, in this measure now before us, is beginning the method of taking the initiative and telling the provinces what it is going to do, then it is just exactly the opposite of what ought to prevail under a federal state; it is undemocratic, it is dictatorial and it is contrary to the British North America Act. It will result ultimately in the destruction of the British North America Act.
I hope I have made clear the general attitude I have in mind when I approach this measure. I strongly suspect, Mr. Chairman, that this method of procedure is the beginning of a mode of approach which will result

in the dominion government taking the initiative, assuming command and telling the provinces what is going to happen. Because I believe that I am going to oppose this resolution with every bit of strength I possess. I believe it would be a good thing for the government to withdraw the resolution and call a provincial conference first. If it takes six weeks, let both parties talk the thing through and come to an understanding. Let the dominion have the provincial premiers put their case and listen. After they put their case then let our Prime Minister say, "What would you provinces suggest as an acceptable method of approach in respect to this matter? Obviously the tax rental agreements have been good for all the provinces, and very likely the tax collection agreement would be, whereby the dominion government collected certain taxes and divided them up amongst the provinces as they, the provinces desired they should be divided."
With that point of view, we the dominion government, say to the provinces, "Well, now, what is the best method of procedure; what is the best formula? How much money is involved? How much do you think we ought to have, because you know quite well, we, the dominion, have to have money to run the country. We have to have money if we are going to do more and more, as we have been doing"-the government has been doing that, and has been doing all the things the hon. member for Charlotte mentioned. All the things he said concerning the benefits which this government has conferred upon the various provinces are true. No one is challenging that.
Well, the Prime Minister would say to the provinces, "Now, you know we must have money and you must have money. Here we have a chance of raising money by taxes, corporation and income tax levies, succession duties. What is your idea?"
There would then be a wide divergence of opinion. I suggest they all should then do just what would be done in any public meeting. They should say, "Let us appoint a committee of the different provinces. Let them take this home, if they want to, and study it. We want this committee to come in and make recommendations that will seem to them equitable and advantageous in the circumstances." What an entirely different method of approach that would be.
The Prime Minister may say, "Well, I have not the time." I do not say he has, but he certainly has plenty of officials who have the time if he would tell them to go in there and listen to the provinces and let all work out the problem with the assistance of the dominion officials in the way of pointing out
16, 1956	S027
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements the difficulties confronting both sides. What difference does it make if it takes more than six weeks, if, at the end of that time, the provinces feel that there has been a straightforward approach to the problem with the objective of getting for everybody concerned the very best solution?
I think possibly I have placed my case before the committee in a general way. There will be those who will disagree. I would be surprised if there were not. I would think there was something wrong with me if everybody agreed with me, nevertheless I think there is a germ there. I have heard a great many people, prominent persons, express very much this same idea.
Now may we turn to the resolution just as it is? I have made this little introductory statement so that people could see what I am driving at. For the members of the committee and for those who will read Hansard out in the country I propose to examine a few aspects of Canadian financial history as those aspects may be related to this particular problem before us.
Meanwhile we have got so far away from the resolution that I think it would be well for me to read it so that those who read these remarks will know what we are talking about. The resolution reads:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide that the Minister of Finance may pay to a province, out of the consolidated revenue fund, in respect of any fiscal year in the period commencing on the first day of April, 1957. and ending on the 31st day of March, 1962
(a)	a tax equalization payment with respect to individual and corporation income taxes and succession duties:
(b)	a provincial revenue stabilization payment with respect to such taxes; and
(c)	a tax rental payment in accordance with a tax rental agreement that may be entered into by any province as an alternative to levying such taxes on its own behalf;
and also to authorize tax collection agreements with the governments of the provinces.
This is the resolution we are talking about. Now, you will know, of course, as those out in the country would not know, that this resolution is the precursor of a contemplated bill, one measure in a considerable series of financial measures in Canada, commencing with the Dominion Notes Act of 1868 and including in the series, first, the Finance Act of 1914; second, the Finance Act of 1923; third, the Bank of Canada Act of 1934; fourth, such acts as have been passed by this house to legalize the tax transfer agreement and the tax rental agreements between the dominion government and the provincial governments which followed the rejection in January, 1941, by the provinces of the proposals recommended by the Rowell-Sirois
6028	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements commission on dominion-provincial relations, set up by Prime Minister King on August 14, 1937. For those who want to find out where the authority is for that, may I refer to Mackenzie King's opening address to the premiers on January 14, 1941, at page 1 of the minutes of proceedings of that conference.
This present resolution appears to mark a new departure. It could be called an introduction to a tax collection agreement. It assumes that the coming dominion-provincial conference upon tax rental agreements will accept once more a dominion-provincial tax rental agreement of the general nature of those already accepted in years gone by, the difference being that this is a tax collection agreement.
It would have appeared more becoming if the conference had been held first and the provinces consulted before the bill was introduced, as I have already pointed out. Thus the provinces would be still in the position of taking the initiative, and the dominion would be acting as an agent for the provinces.
Now, the centralizers just hate the thought of an agent. They talk about the fears that the dominion will fall apart; there will not be any coherence. How in the name of common sense did we "cohere" up to the time the Rowell-Sirois commission was set up? We "cohered" pretty well then. We made a magnificent combination in world war I, and we accomplished a war effort that considering our resources probably surpassed that of any other community on the face of the earth. There was no big stick hanging over us in those days.
What held us together? The love of the union jack; the love of the king; the love of Canada; the love of the dominion; the love of righteousness; the love of Britain. These were the things that held us together, and these are the things that will hold us together in the future, far more solidly than any other consideration like laws, acts or agreements. Therefore those who believe in centralization and who fear that this dominion will fall apart if the central government does not have the power to command them need to revise their opinions in the light of the facts. We Canadian people are people who love great ideals, we people in Canada from coast to coast.
No, I do not hesitate to say that we look upon the dominion as an agent of the provinces put here to do a job for the provinces, just like the democracies in other countries. The government is their agent, their representative that exists for them. They do not conceive of themselves as existing for the government. That is the concept of the
[Mr. Blackmore.l
communist dictator people. Our attitude is entirely different. Therefore I do not hesitate at all to use that expression. Thus the provinces would be well in a position to take the initiative and the dominion would be acting as an agent for the provinces.
Now, then, by mentioning the individual income tax, the corporation income tax and the succession duties, the resolution reminds one of the Rowell-Sirois recommendation. I do not propose to go into that in any great detail at the present time, although I propose to go into details later on. Generally the Rowell-Sirois commission recommended that the provinces vacate income tax, corporation tax and succession duties as fields of taxation, in favour of the dominion, in consideration of certain financial benefits which the dominion would return to them.
I am not going to deal with that in detail at the present time. I am told that my time is up for the present. Therefore I shall make an end of these remarks at the present time, with the promise that when the time comes for me to speak again I shall deal with it then.

Mr. Chairman, it would be superfluous for me to remind the house that we are now discussing one of the most important matters of national interest. Indeed, this year the matter of the federal-provincial financial relations seems to attract much more attention in the other provinces than it has in the past, but for us, citizens of Quebec, that problem always remains our main concern.
This year, the house is called upon to decide on a proposal different no doubt in its form from the proposals made previously by the federal government. First, the amounts offered the provinces by the federal government are a little higher than before; the government will therefore claim that this proposal takes greater account of provincial autonomy than did the previous centralizing proposals, since provinces are given a free hand in the matter of direct taxation: up to 10 per cent of personal income tax, 9 per cent of corporation income tax and 50 per cent of succession duties.
However, Mr. Chairman, this is no solution to the problem, and the amounts that the province of Quebec may receive are totally inadequate for its present and future needs

since the economic and industrial development now going on in Quebec is but a beginning. Moreover, the constitutional rights resulting from confederation are no more respected than they were before.
Naturally, we could hardly expect a complete change of policy after the famous speeches delivered by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on board the Saxonia and at the Reform Club, when he tried, in the strongest terms, to ridicule the stand taken by the government of the province of Quebec on that matter. Besides, this centralizing stand was reaffirmed by the four other federal ministers from Quebec and by the non-co-operating Liberal members, as my friend Mr. Mongrain called them during the last provincial electoral campaign.
They bore down heavily on the autonomous policy of Mr. Duplessis. They jested mightily about it, with results that are now rather well known.
While federal Liberal ministers and members did their utmost to belittle, in the eyes of the electors, the decentralizing policy of Quebec's premier, their provincial leader, Mr. Lapalme, stated on the same hustings that the federal government owed the province of Quebec $300 million which he promised to recover should the provincial Liberal party be elected. However, we must admit that the federal Liberal members did not say much on that point; they did not insist upon it, any more than they talked about the matter of the Chateau Maisonneuve, which only they can settle.
In fact, the resolution moved by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) and upon which we are called upon to pass judgment, is not the result of a conference between the federal government and the provinces; not at all. We are not being asked to ratify an agreement between the dominion government and the provinces, an agreement reached following long negotiations where every party concerned had previously examined the proposals made. On the contrary, once again the federal government acted in a centralizing and unilateral way. It called the provinces together, read its proposal and asked them what they thought about it, made a few minor changes here and there and said: "Do as you wish; this is as far as we can go," knowing full well that the provinces are not in a position to do without them, even though they found the amounts altogether inadequate.

The federal government proposes the 10, 9 and 50 per cent formula with equalization, but warns the provinces that it does not intend to add one cent. If you want more money, it is very simple, all you have to do is to levy additional taxes, or increase the present ones. If your municipalities are overburdened by heavy expenditures, and if your school boards cannot supply all the necessary schools and class rooms for a school population that has nearly doubled in the past fifteen years, the only thing to do is to levy new taxes or increase your taxes on real estate, even though those taxes are already too high and have long exceeded the limit.
As for the federal government, it dries up all other sources of taxation but says to the provinces and municipalities: "Levy new taxes", as if the provincial and municipal taxpayers were not the same taxpayers who are already so regularly and thoroughly fleeced by the federal government. As if those taxpayers were living in Africa! No, Mr. Chairman, those taxpayers who live in municipalities and in the provinces are the same ones who are faced with urgent needs; they are the same ones who must pay excessive taxes to the federal government, which is wallowing in wealth.

Mr. Chairman, prior to the dinner adjournment at six o'clock, I was saying that the federal government was wallowing in wealth while the provincial governments and the municipalities were facing the greatest difficulties. Here in Ottawa surpluses have been recorded practically every year since the end of the war, and these surpluses of $100 million, $200 million or $300 million which have been accumulated since the war now reach a total of close to $2 billion. That is an extravagant figure, and even this year many experienced people claim that the federal government may end the year with a surplus of close to three-quarters of a billion dollars.
That means, Mr. Chairman, that the federal government will have overtaxed the provincial and municipal taxpayers to the tune of $750 million, which makes absolutely no sense. And the proof that it does not make

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements sense is that the federal government feels so rich that it rushes into adventures as scandalous as its gifts and its loans of more than $150 million to the pipe lines of Mr. Murchison and his friends in the United States.
These much talked of surpluses, Mr. Chairman, are piled up by this government at the expense of the provinces and the municipalities themselves. If this country is now experiencing an unheard of industrial development, which in turn fills the coffers of the Minister of Finance, it is due first of all to the provinces which are called upon to make the first disbursement, though they have to wait long after the federal government has helped itself, before they get anything out of it.
If you want examples, they are very easy to find. Take the case of all the new industries which come and settle in the towns of our province. First, the municipality has to ensure water, sewer, street or road services, garbage collection, snow removal, schools, etc. Most of the time, the municipalities have to grant tax exemptions and seek assistance from the provincial governments for the establishment of each of the municipal services, and, finally, the provincial governments have to help school commissions give these new developments new school buildings almost every year.
After all those expenses caused by a new development have been made, the federal government establishes mail service for instance, but here again, only after receiving delegation after delegation, after requesting that a sidewalk be built and that there should not be more than 80 feet between one house and the next, that the federal government agrees to provide letter-carrier service, even if it takes only one hour per day, at a cost of approximately $500. It is probably the only immediate expense that would be incurred by the federal government in a new development.
And all the time the plant is being built, the federal government,-which did not have to pay a single cent for this new development, collects the sales taxes on materials, income tax from the first pay day of each worker, and so on; and later on it collects taxes on corporation profits as soon as the manufacturer is making any money.
For a more concrete instance, take the case of Chibougamau.

The province of Quebec had to build a road costing more than $6 million from St. Feli-cien to Chibougamau, right in the middle of the woods, where there was not a living soul, and even before a single ton of ore could be processed. This road enabled an absolutely virgin area to become one of the most important mining centres of this country. Out of the pay cheque of each miner, out of the profits of each of these companies that were developing the fields, the federal government took the lion's share before the province even received a cent, though it was the province that had paid so much to bring this new development into being.
When everything was done and the strides of mining would have called for the building of a railway, it had to be demanded for years in this house. The companies, the chamber of commerce of the Lake St. John district, and the municipalities had to prove with figures to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) that the federal government could make a profit as soon as this railway was established. The companies were even asked to give written undertakings before the government agreed to build this railroad-

Even when those gentlemen of the Department of Transport and of the Canadian National Railways had all the necessary evidence on hand, they required a further six months to think it over before they agreed to invest funds in a venture the outcome of which could no longer be doubted by anyone.

Labrieville, Havre St-Pierre, Schefferville, all those municipalities are mushrooming, producing for the country and paying taxes that are increasing steadily each year.

Cities are built, schools go up by the hundreds and the federal government gets millions of dollars out of it while the provincial government spends its funds. And if you ask for a railway to link this new industrial empire to other parts of the country, the Minister of Transport says you are a dreamer.

To give another example concerning my riding, I am going to mention the harbour of Three Rivers, one of the few whose operation is paying the federal government a profit.
The Three Rivers harbour, Mr. Chairman, lacks modern equipment and sheds. Very often the goods of our manufacturers are left on the wharves, exposed to rain and weather, because of the lack of sheds. The amount that the federal government proposes to spend on improvements to this harbour, from which it derived millions of dollars, is $35,000, and this only after the representations of the chamber of commerce of Three Rivers, and those of municipal authorities, which I have been echoing in this house.
Do you know what the chairman of the national harbours board said when the board sat at Three Rivers? This gentleman told us emphatically that if new companies in Three Rivers needed additional wharves, the board would not impede that development and would make sure that they be given to those companies once they are established there.
The federal government, which does not want to give up its privileged position as far as taxation is concerned, a position in which it has entrenched itself during two world wars, always resorts to the same pretext, national defence.
Every time anyone talks about income tax reductions, the government answers that it is impossible on account of national defence. Whenever public works are required that would help industrial development, we are told that it is impossible because of national defence. And whenever the provinces ask for more generous treatment by the federal government, they too are told that it is impossible on account of national defence. However, although the necessary national defence expenditures are high, at present, they are not likely to increase as the years go by, while the expenditures that the provinces must assume in order to ensure the industrial development of Canada are and will be steadily increasing from year to year.
Besides, is it not obvious that Russia tends to transform her threat of military conflict of these last years into a threat of economic domination. And the western countries, such as England, are going to reduce their war budget, their national defence expenditure, to undertake a greater economic development.

Canada will no doubt have to follow that example, and while federal defence expenditures will be on the wane, the provinces will have to face the prospect of economic warfare and pay the costs of it should the present fiscal agreements remain in force.
The Minister of Finance makes much of the fact that one of the most interesting features of the present federal proposals is that the province of Quebec will be in a position to receive the same amounts as the other provinces without having to sign any agreements to that effect, agreements which the people of Quebec province would never, in fact, have signed, as was so often demonstrated in the past.
It is high time that the people of Quebec should cease to be placed in an inferior financial position and to lose vast sums of money simply because its government, answering the all but unanimous views of the people, has refused to be a party to agreements which run counter to its traditions, to the traditions of the province, to its autonomy and to those rights guaranteed to it by the constitution of this country. However, the proposals brought down by the Minister of Finance in this resolution do not solve the problem within the meaning and the spirit of the constitution, not even for the next few years. What is in fact required is a federal-provincial conference in which the federal government and the provinces will consider the steps to be taken for a fair distribution of taxation fields, so that the provinces may play their part in their own sphere. As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) so aptly stated, the power of taxation means the power to govern, and the government of the province of Quebec must enjoy its own powers of taxation so as to be able to administer that province which, no matter what is said, is different from the others because of its language and its faith.
Education is the guarantee of the survival and development of the French Canadian race on the North American continent, and it is the duty of the Quebec government to preserve it with jealous care. To do so, it must have the power to legislate on all matters pertaining to education within the province. The power to legislate cannot operate soundly without the power to tax for the same ends, and that power cannot operate soundly if the province is at the mercy of the central government's subsidies.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, while the federal proposals are an improvement as far

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements as the amounts to be paid the provinces are concerned, I consider first that these amounts are inadequate to meet the enormous responsibilities of the provinces in the economic development of the country, of which they are the main architects.

For these reasons, Mr. Chairman, I will vote against the resolution of the Minister of Finance.

Mr. Chairman, I feel rather hesitant in rising to my feet after the display of emotional oratory we have just heard. I do not blame the hon. gentleman a particle, because this is something which should arouse deep feelings. My only regret is that I will not be able to do justice to it. What the minister said in introducing the resolution did not salve my feelings a particle when he used phrases such as "implement the offer." That is good proof of what we claim this to be, that it is nothing less than an offer by the federal government to the provinces and is not anything in the nature of an agreement as we are given to understand it is.
Then we heard the phrase "allow the provinces." That is another phrase I do not like. I do not think it is up to this central government to allow the provinces any rights so far as taxation is concerned. These tax rights were granted to them many years ago when this confederation was first born, and I do not think phrases such as that help to ease a situation which to say the least is packed with dynamite.
Those speakers who have spoken thus far have certainly covered the ground quite fully, and it is rather hard to find something new to bring up. The Leader of the Opposition did a splendid job this morning in outlining the general principles on which our opposition to the bill to follow this resolution should be based. The resolution states:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide that the Minister of Finance may pay to a province, out of the consolidated revenue fund-
I do not like that "pay to a province, out of the consolidated revenue fund." I should like to ask a question. Where does the money come from that is placed in the consolidated revenue fund? Is it not money that has been collected from the various provinces and the people who reside in them? A sentence such as that would give the impression that a dole is being handed back to the provinces from this general revenue fund. It may be a payment from the consolidated revenue fund, but in my opinion it is nothing more nor less than a refund of a small part of the money the central government has collected from the provinces.
Then we come to paragraph (c) of the resolution, which says:
(c) a tax rental payment in accordance with a tax rental agreement that may be entered into by any province as an alternative to levying such taxes on its own behalf;
There is talk there of an agreement, but from what we can gather from the expressions of opinion in the different provinces from one side of Canada to the other it is very doubtful if there will be any agreement. If an agreement is made, how has it been reached? Further, I cannot see any possibility of this being anything more than a one-sided agreement to which the federal government alone agrees. Then why the rush in introducing this legislation at the present time? Why not wait until there is an agreement?
I wonder if there is any sinister motive, such as the idea that the central government can go to the provinces, once the bill following this resolution has been passed by the house, and say, "This is what has been passed by the parliament of Canada. It is up to the various provinces to attach their signature to it in order to close out what has been approved by this parliament as representative of the people." I think possibly that is the principal motive, in order to strengthen their hand in the forthcoming settlement which, at the present time, is very far off. I do not like this idea of the strong voice or playing from strength in so far as the central government is concerned.
The increasing authority this government are placing in their own hands is, step by step, vesting in this government the sole right to tax. There have been various other infringements of provincial rights which we have seen during the past few years. We are all well aware of the old saying that the right to tax is the right to govern, and what will follow this measure will certainly take away from the provinces the right to tax and substitute therefor the right of the federal government to perform all functions. There is also an old saying that whoever collects and handles the money will want to call the tune.


Now that the right of taxation is being delegated to the central government, where are the rights of the provinces? What has become of provincial autonomy about which we heard so much? This whole problem, Mr. Chairman, of federal-provincial relations and it is a problem-is to my mind being approached in the wrong way. In my opinion the provinces of Canada should be calling this conference and not the central government, just as at the time of confederation it was the provinces which called the conference to set up this central government. It is from the provinces of Canada that this central government receives its authority. I maintain that this still is an institution, and should always remain an institution, to carry out the wishes and the will of the provinces of Canada and the people who live in those provinces.
I agree that it is sound policy to have one collection agency. The way to have that agency set up would be for the provinces and the federal government to get together and work out some plan for the collection of these taxes through one central agency. Instead of that, at the present time we have the central government saying in effect, "We have decided that we shall collect all taxes on a national basis for the next five years, and we shall pay you a small percentage of what we collect in the provinces. A formula has been arrived at. We have carefully figured this out. If you want to accept it, it is there for your signature. It is our only offer, so take it or leave it".
Where is the idea of confederation about which we heard so much in the early days when this country had its birth? I am satisfied that if those statesmen who gathered around the conference table some 89 years ago-Macdonald, Brown, Tupper and Cartier -could see the turn events have taken since their day they would not be too well pleased. What would they think of the central government imposing its will and authority upon the provinces which they were so careful to agree should retain autonomy within the federation?
When a conference is called, it should be called to consider this whole problem. I believe all the provinces should be given an opportunity to lay their cards on the table. They have their problems. They have revenues to find to cover such things as health, mental institutions and so on. They need money for universities and technical training, a serious problem which was raised here today. They need money for roads, bridges, public buildings and all that sort of thing. Why not have all the authorities get together and lay that information on the

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements table, then come to some kind of an agreement? It could be a tax rental agreement, or whatever you like to call it, and these points could be considered. We could work in harmony and close co-operation in the setting up of this single agency for the collection of taxes, but we should see that sufficient was left in the coffers or returned to the coffers of the various provinces in order to take care of those things I have mentioned.
It is not only the poor provinces but some of the wealthiest provinces that are having considerable trouble financing the increasing demand for services. This is a nation-wide problem which extends right from the Pacific to the Atlantic. It is not only in the federal field that the cost of government has increased. In fact we find that the increase in the cost of the federal government has been much less than for provincial and municipal governments.
For instance, in 1945 the expenditure of the federal government was $4,527 million. In 1955 it was $4,733 million, an increase of 5-5 per cent. In 1945 the total cost of the provincial governments across Canada was $384 million. In 1955 it had risen to $1,505 million, an increase of 293 per cent. Just think of that. In 1945 the municipalities, Mr. Chairman, had a total cost of operation amounting to $344 million. In 1955, 10 years later, it was $1,293 million, an increase of 276 per cent.
These figures show that we have federal increases in the cost of government of 5-5 per cent, provincial increases of 292 per cent and municipal increases of 276 per cent. This is something that must be given very careful consideration. Under the staggering costs these figures show, what can the provinces and municipal tax collecting agencies do when they find that their fields of taxation are being encroached upon by the federal authorities? They might well ask themselves, where is this money to come from?
There is one field of expenditure in my own province that I should like to spend a few moments on, and that is the matter of roads. The government of British Columbia has set up a five-year program for the building of roads into forest areas known as public working circles of that province. In the next five years they are committed to build 1,460 miles of roads. The total cost of those roads is going to be $41,350,000.
It is true that the British Columbia government will get some revenues from the forests that are tapped by those access roads, but what about the huge taxation that will also accrue to the federal government through access being provided and those areas opened up? It is estimated that in the area which

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements those roads will serve there will be a yearly take from the forest of $64,787,916. The total for the five years is estimated to be $323,939,580. From that staggering amount, Mr. Chairman, the central government is going to collect, by way of income and corporation taxes, a huge amount of money; yet in opening up those areas not a five cent piece will be given toward the staggering cost of $41,350,000.
Then we have our arterial highways and bridges. For these they have set up in the province of British Columbia a 20-year program. There are yet to be built 2,086 miles. The estimated cost of that program is $397,500,000. In that 2,086 miles are included 350 miles of the trans-Canada highway. The central government is contributing toward that. I am very glad to say that road will go through the most expensive area of British Columbia, so far as road-building cost is concerned, and I think a very wise decision has been made in that respect. There we have an outlay on arterial highways of $397,500,000 for the next 20 years.
But that is not all. There are also other, what we call in British Columbia pioneer roads, opening up new areas in the north and districts that have not yet been reached by highways. That mileage cost in the next 20 years will be $498,500,000 and the number of miles will be 3,530. If we add these together, Mr. Chairman, we find that for the next 20 years the province of British Columbia is faced with an annual cost of $44,800,000. That is the cost at present.
Those new roads that are being built into the undeveloped areas will tap the forest resources, the mineral resources, the gas and oil resources of the north, and the new agricultural areas. It is true there will be some wealth accrue to the government of British Columbia, but at the same time millions of new money will find its way into the treasury of the central government as a result of the opening up and the development of those areas, yet of the expenditure of $44,800,000 annually not a five cent piece will be contributed by this central government.
Then, of course, we come on down to what we call our country and feeder roads. I have not the figures on these, but I know it is a staggering amount. Of course that is something that is the problem of the municipalities and the smaller local governments of the province of British Columbia. I think it is only right that in arriving at any agreements with the provinces items such as these should be given consideration and should be taken into account.
I agree there should be a plan to assist the so-called have-not provinces, but this should

be done by building up the poorer provinces, not by tearing down the standards of the wealthy and more industrialized provinces. The old socialist slogan, even accepted by some today, and voiced in parliament since I came here, is that in order to make the poor richer the rich must be made poorer. This is just as outdated as socialism itself. It is not right that in this modern age, in approaching the question of balancing the standards of living, you might say, among the provinces, this same method should be followed. It is certainly not the ideal of free enterprise which we in this country profess to believe in; yet in reaching an agreement such as we have before us at the present time that is the system which is being used.
To back that up I should like to read a paragraph from the brief presented by the province of British Columbia on federal-provincial fiscal relations, just to show the committee that this is not my idea alone:
British Columbia has constantly advocated financial assistance to provinces in depressed economic circumstances, but there is a vast difference between one method of securing greater equality and another. One way is to level up; the other is to level down. One way is to raise the real income of the worse off without endangering the standards of living of those with special abilities who have the means to provide greater awards. The other is to deprive this group of the gains which would accrue from ability and potential worth.
Yet that is the policy which is being adopted by the central government in their approach to the problem we are considering at the present time. Wo believe that where there is criticism there should be some suggestions. I do not think it is right and correct for a person to stand up and tear down unless he has something to offer in return. I should like to present two or three suggestions for consideration. First, with respect to this resolution, I would like to see the whole thing done away with except the last line, which reads:
To authorize tax collection agreements with the governments of the provinces.
I would say the only way to arrive at such agreement is for them to gather around a conference table and sit there for days and weeks if necessary until an agreement is reached. Second, immediately call another conference with all the provinces and give sympathetic attention to the varying needs of the provinces, and careful consideration to all problems that are in the national interest such as education, health, highways, highway transportation and development of natural resources that are in the national interest. Third-and this is the most important; it is the environment under which these agreements are reached-endeavour at this

conference table to create a spirit of cooperation and let the provinces know that the spirit of confederation is not dead; that there is still such a thing as provincial rights, and that the federal government exists for the sole purpose of discharging the duty of administering the affairs of Canada in the interests of all the people of Canada and of all the provinces of Canada in which those people live.

Mr. Chairman, like other hon. members who have spoken to this resolution I too am greatly interested in the legislation. As the minister said this morning in his opening remarks, we all know pretty much what it is going to contain. I was rather hoping he was not going to make such a definite statement, that an opportunity would still be left for bargaining and that it would not appear that an agreement was going to follow as a result of the legislation from which rightly or wrongly one gets the impression that the government is saying, "We will offer you this and if you do not like it you do not have to take it".
That just does not seem to me to be the way an agreement should be arrived at. An agreement is usually arrived at through a meeting of minds, and each party has an opportunity to present his views. I do not mean to imply that the provinces were not given an opportunity to discuss the matter, but from reports of the conferences that were held I cannot help but gather the impression that while the provinces were permitted to put forward their cases, their formulas and problems were not given the consideration I feel they should have been given because- and this is the ground on which I base my statement-if the provinces' propositions had been given consideration I do not think the premiers and officials of the provinces would have returned home and said that the offer which the Prime Minister submitted in his letter of January 6 was not sufficient to meet the needs and carry out the services of the provinces, which are fair and reasonable under the Canadian standard of living, or words to that effect.
The resolution itself, of course, is leading up to enabling legislation. I do not think there is any reason why it should not be brought in at this time. I do not agree with one of the speakers who suggested that the legislation should not be brought in. I can see no reason for not bringing it in, because it is enabling legislation. It seems to me, however, that the government should convince us that they are going to be fair in the agreements they present, and will give the provinces a fair opportunity to present their cases if they want us to support this

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements resolution. The government should assure us that the views of the provinces will be considered and that through negotiation and by compromise something will be arrived at that is satisfactory to at least the majority of the premiers of the various provinces. As I understand the situation as it exists today, they are not satisfied.
Perhaps I could just digress for a moment. This whole matter arose in the dark days of the war when it seemed right for all the resources of this country to have been concentrated in a central authority in order to successfully prosecute the struggle in which we were then engaged, which was a life and death struggle involving Canada and her allies. At that time the provinces and municipalities under the agreements entered into were guaranteed as much as they had been collecting up to that time. During the latter years of the war and up until 1946 or 1947, when the agreements ran out, the people became accustomed to the system of single taxation. In many cases the provinces did away with the administrative machinery they had used to collect revenue, and as I said the people became accustomed to the single taxation system. In effect I think it was more equitable. I feel the central government has a better and fairer method of collecting income tax and succession duties, because it is sitting here like the head of a family. I believe it is true that the people would rather pay into one treasury than into several.
One opinion was extremely well expressed by Mr. Matheson, the premier of Prince Edward Island, during the negotiations last fall among the various governments. I am going to quote his words, because I think he expressed the feeling of the maritime premiers and the people of those provinces concerning the renewal of these agreements at the end of the war. This is what he said:
In 1946 we-
Referring to the provinces.
-accepted the tax rental agreement offer-
Notice that, "the tax rental agreement offer". You cannot get away from the idea, whether or not it is correct, that these have been offers, which have been presented to the provinces by the federal government, which has said, "That is all we can do; take it or leave it." Mr. Matheson said they accepted it:
. . . not because It represented some recognition of fiscal need but with a hope that during the lifetime of that agreement a more satisfactory formula would be devised. In 1952 the federal government proposed a new guaranteed minimum payment based on the one allotted to a province under the 1947 agreement with an increase proportionate to change in provincial population and per capita gross national product between 1942 and 1948.
