He continued:
No recognition of a province's fiscal need problem or its tax-raising ability was taken into consideration in the reallocation or distribution of the tax moneys, but the same old factors were again used in the formula-the gross national product of Canada and the population of the provinces.
He concluded:
One of the principal functions of the tax rental agreements was that they were to ease the finances of the provincial governments possessing the lowest fiscal capacity.
Rightly or wrongly I believe that was the principle that was supposed to have been followed under the tax rental agreements from the beginning. The underlying principle was to make it financially possible for provinces whatever their tax base to carry out and perform their constitutional functions, and to provide a reasonable level of provincial services without abnormal burdens of taxation. This includes the province's responsibilities to the municipalities.
That brings me to another point I should like to mention. It has been stressed a great deal by all the speakers today, but I should like to say something further about it and I hope to approach it from a different angle. You may say that I am municipal minded. You may think I am altogether wrong. Perhaps I am; nevertheless I have views, and I know they are shared by many others.
The municipalities must be kept in mind when these agreements are entered into. With all respect, it seems to me that these negotiations between the provincial and the federal authorities have started from the wrong premise. I shall try to explain that. It seems to me that the governments have approached this from the top and gone down. To me the proper method of approach in arriving at any agreement which is going to give the people any relief from taxation and a fair division of the tax moneys collected from the people of this country is to start at the bottom.
It seems to me the first thing that should be done is that the provinces should be asked to lay before the federal authorities the requirements of their municipalities in so far as the real necessities that must be furnished by the municipalities to the people are concerned. We are all very familiar with those services which are the primary responsibility in so far as the taxpayers in our communities are concerned; education, hospitalization, roads, streets, water, sewage disposal, police and fire departments, and to a large extent the administration of justice. Those are essential services. I think the people of Canada have a right to expect a certain level of those services all across this country under


our constitutional set-up. I believe that has been brought out more than once by various commissions.
Therefore I am sorry I cannot agree with my hon. friend from Charlotte. I do not think the people are going to be satisfied, and I am very mild in that statement; because I feel, and a good many of us feel, that we in New Brunswick and in Prince Edward Island and in Nova Scotia deserve just as good schools, and our teachers should be paid just as much money; we should receive just as good equipment; our young people getting an education should have the same privileges as they would have in Ontario or any other province where they have a much broader base on which to assess. In a province like one of those in the east, the federal income tax people collect our income tax, which seems to come first; the corporations have to pay corporation tax; and the estates have to pay succession duty tax. Of course that does not come into municipal matters.
But take the municipal tax collector. The municipality has to assess for those schools, for the buildings, for the teachers, for the equipment, for the transportation. They have to find ways and means of getting that money, and the money must come from earnings. Earnings will depend very much on the type of industry in the locality. In our province we have to resort to poll taxes, which some provinces do not have to resort to. We have to resort to personal property tax in order to raise money locally to provide the best service we can in the way of education, hospitalization and these other services.
In rural municipalities it used to be that education did not cost very much. In fact I remember quite well that even in the period after the war the cost of running the schools in the municipality where I used to live was in the vicinity of $60,000 to $70,000. Last January the budget presented to the municipality for the same area was over $400,000. Even though, as Premier Matheson has said, the dominion did not take into consideration the fiscal needs, they may not have been impressed upon the federal authorities in 1946 because the period 1946-47 was when these costs commenced to rise. Prior to that, as I have just pointed out, the cost of education was rather a small item. It has kept going up until now it is a very large item. Still we have no more resources to tax. Our tax base is very narrow. Once the income tax is taken and the corporation tax is taken, we have to look to the province for the balance.
I am not going to criticize or brag about what our province has done. I am not familiar with what others have done, but I know,

because I have been connected with municipal governments right along, that our province has increased grants to the municipalities by a very considerable amount. As my hon. friend from Charlotte says, percentagewise it has not increased so much. I have no complaint about that, but they have received enormous sums. The point is that everything else has increased. The province has to spend more money on other essential services, and the revenue is taken up in meeting those other services.
That brings me to another point which I think should be mentioned. I notice that in that report there is an extensive list of services rendered by the dominion and the provincial governments, services in the fields of health, welfare, and education to some extent but not in the most necessary fields of education; it is for vocational training mainly. Then there is the field of agriculture and the field of national resources, for which there is quite an extensive table. However, what the provinces have to do is to meet those services dollar for dollar. I believe most of them are essential, but I feel that some of the services in that list, which the federal government has been offering to the people through the provinces on a share basis, are not as essential as education, health and justice.
There is another point I should like to mention. First, I claim that this federal authority and the provincial governments should find out the essential needs of the municipalities to provide at least the minimum service at the level of what we might call a Canadian standard of living.
Second, I think there should be an investigation into the essential provincial services that have to be rendered to the people in order to keep the province abreast of what the people expect by way of roads, bridges and various other things. I know we have a tremendous number of bridges in my province, and it is very expensive to maintain them. In addition, so many of the old roads are narrow. Demands are made for wider roads, and we also have heavier equipment using our roads today such as buses, trucks and so on. These are all essential provincial services.
Having established these minimum essential services, I claim that the federal government should then commence to consider what their minimum requirements are. After all, there is only one source of taxation and it is very foolish for two or three governments to try to see which one can get there first or get the most. I think it should be a sensible thing to sit down and say that those are essential, those are essential and we have certain other essential services. But after
16, 1956	6039
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements sitting here for four years and looking at some of the estimates I am satisfied, and I cannot be convinced otherwise, that the government can tighten its belt and furnish the essential services that are required with a lot less money than is being spent now.
There is one other factor I wish to mention. Industries from which income taxes and other revenues are collected settle in a municipality and the first government they contact is the municipal government. 1 know that the practice to which I am about to refer has been carried on over the past years and I know that, rightly or wrongly, it is still going on. I do not say it is right and I would not be surprised if the Minister of Finance said it was not the fault of the federal government and that it was wrong in principle. However, the fact is that when an industry settles in a municipality it immediately approaches the municipal governing body and asks for tax concessions. In many instances those concessions have been granted by municipalities in order to encourage industry to settle there. They have been granted in order to assist industry to get going.
But after they have got started, are doing well and are progressing, who gets the first returns? It is the federal government. They get them through corporation taxes and through income tax paid by the people who work in those industries. Then the municipality, which has to furnish the services for the industry, has to tax the land and the people. The municipality has to come second. As all members know, there is a limit to the extent to which you can assess real estate in the form of land; and I say without fear of contradiction, and I know hon. members from the province will support me, that in my province the municipalities have reached a point in taxing real estate beyond which we have no right to go. In fact it is a point beyond which it is not safe to go, because the people cannot afford to pay more taxes and retain their real estate. It will be cheaper to let the municipality take it.
These tax concessions are a fact and I think they should be taken into consideration when negotiations are being carried on between the provincial and federal authorities. In some instances the municipal authorities grant tax concessions to industries extending over a period of 20 or 25 years in order to keep the industries there, and during that period the municipalities fail to realize revenue from them. Rightly or wrongly, it is a fact and it should be taken into consideration.
I say again that I feel we start at the wrong place when we start at the top and go down. It seems to me that is exactly
6040	HOUSE OF
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements where these negotiations have been starting. The federal authorities figure out how much they must have to maintain their services, and then they say there is only so much left. Education, health and the administration of justice are three things that take a lot of municipal revenue. In case some of you do not know, may I say that it is surprising how much a municipality has to raise for the administration of justice in order to furnish the buildings and provide other things. As I say, I do not think these three things should have any boundaries.
I think every child and every other person in Canada should have an equal opportunity to acquire an education. Under the framework of our constitution this responsibility of course rests upon the municipal authority. That is why it seems to me that in all fairness we should find out what the essential services are and how much money it is going to take to provide a reasonable standard of education, a reasonable standard of health and a reasonable standard of justice throughout the nation. That would be one place to start.
I think there is a good foundation to be found for this argument in the past, and also good reason for us to be talking about it today. Reference has been made once or twice to the Rowell-Sirois report. There is a quotation from that report which seems to me to be applicable. It is to be found in chapter 5 of book 2, and has to do with adjustment grants about which I intend to say something later. It has this to say:
They are designed to make it possible for every province to provide for its people services of average Canadian standards and they will thus alleviate distress and shameful conditions which now weaken national unity and handicap many Canadians. They are the concrete expression of the commission's conception of a federal system which will both preserve a healthy local autonomy and build a stronger and more united nation.
That brings me to the second part of my remarks. According to the premiers, and they should know best, these agreements are not sufficient to bring the people of the provinces up to the standard of living which I think Canadians should expect. As a matter of fact I do not think they measure up by any means to the declaration of the Prime Minister when he set out what he thought- and I agree with him-was the intention of these agreements. His remarks are to be found in one of the letters and are set out at page 747 of Hansard of January 31, 1956. I think this is a declaration which should be lived up to, and if I felt it was being lived up to so far as the provinces are concerned I could very readily support the legislation that will follow this resolution. He said:

The present government has no intention of abandoning the objective of the tax rental agreements which is to make it financially possible for all the provinces whatever their tax base to perform their constitutional functions themselves and to provide a reasonable Canadian level of provincial services without an abnormal burden, of taxation.
That is in line with the Rowell-Sirois report; it is in line with what I said at the beginning I thought the idea was when they started out with these agreements. I think the agreements have been a good thing, and I think the maritime provinces want these agreements renewed. As a citizen of one of those provinces I believe it is far better to have agreements than to be compelled to go back into these fields of taxation, because we have such a narrow tax base.
We have no resources to tax, that is as yet. Unless the principle which has been recognized has been carried out, we will be faced with difficulties. In order to carry that out it seems to me that you have to go right back to my suggestion. You have to find out how much is required by the municipalities for education, hospitals, streets, roads, fire protection and so on. You have to find out what it is necessary for the provinces to do. When that has been arrived at-and there may have to be some compromise but I think it can be worked out-you have a point at which to begin. It seems to me that it could not have been approached from that standpoint or we would not have had all our premiers dissatisfied.
There is another situation we have in the maritimes which in my opinion does not apply in some of the other provinces. We were the original partners in confederation, and as was stated in the Rowell-Sirois report succession duties, income tax and corporation tax were considered as national taxes which should go into the national revenue. I agree with that. I believe the central authority can do the best job of collecting; but just because it can do that job of collecting, just because it got into that tax field during the war and finds it is a grand place to get money, is in my opinion no reason why it should want to hang on to it. I submit the provinces must be given sufficient so they can provide a reasonable Canadian level of provincial services, as set out in the Prime Minister's declaration. The formula which I understand will be incorporated in the legislation to follow is not going to do that.
Therefore I cannot see how I can support this legislation or any legislation that follows unless I have some assurance on behalf of my people that we are going to have sufficient money out of these agreements to permit us


to provide the same level of services which the richer and more fortunate provinces can provide. There are one or two other things I wanted to mention, but I believe my time is up.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to take part in the debate on this resolution tonight because the municipalities in the county which I have the honour to represent are finding that the revenue they are able to collect from real property is not sufficient. They are taking all they feel they can take, and the squeeze is getting tighter and tighter because of the increased need for new surveys, roads, bridges and educational facilities.
I do not propose to go into all the details of these agreements which have been brought out today, as I think they have been covered pretty well pro and con, nor do I propose to go into their history. I well remember that in 1945 one of the things I was asked to digest was the Rowell-Sirois report. Even to this day I have not been able to take in all its ramifications. However, I do propose to bring to the minister's attention some of the things which are happening in the municipalities. I mention the municipalities particularly because they are less able to expand their tax base than either the provinces or the dominion.
I would point out that no government can give anything until it takes something away from someone. While there may be three different levels of government doing the taxing, there is still only the one taxpayer, the one source of income. I think it was pointed out quite well today that the responsibilities of the federal government have been expanded and extended since the close of the war. No one can question the increased amount of social services which have been asked for, no doubt with more to be added. No one can question very much our expenditures on national defence. I think everyone is worried about the future as far as national defence is concerned, but I do think we have less to show for our national defence dollar than for any dollar spent by the municipality. I believe the municipality can show more for its tax dollar than any other taxing authority in the country.
We must consider the tax revenue which the municipalities receive and compare it with the services they provide in the way of education, roads and other things. I have here a breakdown of what one municipality does with the money it collects. Another thing we must realize that is out of every tax dollar collected, only 11 per cent is used by the municipality. That should make us
16, 1956	6041
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements wonder that they are able to do as much as they do with the little they get.
In the case of the municipality in which I live, 25 per cent of its tax dollar goes to the county; 45 per cent is used for schools, and only 30 per cent is used for township purposes. They have very little to use of the tax dollar they collect after the schools have taken 45 per cent and the county another 25 per cent.
People think rigid economy on the part of the federal government could provide some saving, but I suppose the minister will ask me where they should start. I find that with an election not too far away surpluses are piling up. Probably that is not attributable so much to the government's good housekeeping as to the increase in the gross national product which has taken place.
As I pointed out in the beginning, the municipal governments are really the weakest. They are not able to expand their tax base, nor are they able to demand from provincial or federal governments a much greater share of the tax dollar. The situation has become so serious in some municipalities that they are discouraging the opening up of new subdivisions and that, in a sense, is rather serious. These municipalities feel that for the time being they had better consolidate their position and let some other municipality take the influx of population and also carry the burden so far as schools, roads and other services are concerned. As the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton so ably pointed out, the municipality has to take care of education, streets, hospitalization, water supplies and sewage disposal. Those are only a few of the items.
When it comes to the question of water in southwestern Ontario, we are almost surrounded by the great lakes but the water supply problem is quite acute. The water resources committee of the province of Ontario is trying to aid the municipalities in securing water supplies in a co-operative way, in order that many municipalities can take advantage of the abundance of water that surrounds them. Then there are other municipalities which, in a sense, are stealing water right from under another municipality and selling that water back to the same municipality. They are also dumping the water back into the municipality in the form of a kind of diluted sewage, to the detriment of the neighbouring municipalities along the rivers or streams of the province. Municipalities are hesitating about installing improved sewage disposal facilities because of the tax rates. They realize that when these additional improvements are made, the tax rate must go up.

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements
There is another aspect of the problem of which all levels of government should ndt lose sight. When taxes are imposed on a land owner, he cannot pass them on to anyone. The taxes at other levels can become part of the cost of doing business, and they also become a part of the cost of goods that go into the export market. When the level of taxes becomes too high we find ourselves in a difficult position. I realize, of course, that taxes only become a small part of the cost of manufactured goods, but they are a part.
Now, I do not suppose anyone realizes the impact of all these problems better than the reeves and mayors of the various municipalities in the province. I do not intend at this time to go into the details of the various resolutions the reeves and mayors have placed before the various governments, but they are the ones who are closest to the people and their resolutions should be seriously considered.
There has been considerable said in the press and other places about United States investment in Canadian resources. I am just going to digress for a moment to point out that if more of the Canadian taxpayers' earned income were left in their pockets, more Canadian dollars would be available for investment in Canadian resources. I want to point out also that the federal government should be exemplary in its own tax-paying policies. The percentage of tax the federal government pays on its property should be 100 per cent, not a percentage depending on the concentration of federal properties in any one municipality. The federal government, in my estimation, should be in no different position from the ordinary taxpayers in this country. Why should they be in a preferred class? Some time ago there was a reference in the newspapers to a municipality on Manitoulin island that was threatening to sell some government property for taxes. I have not heard anything about it lately, but probably the minister will say something about it when he replies to the various criticisms that have been hurled at this resolution.

I mentioned earlier that it seemed strange how surpluses develop about the third or fourth year of any parliament. However, I have noticed that the surpluses are never used to alleviate the problems of the municipalities. The government always seems able to find what appears to be a better use for the money. I think it was back in 1953 or 1954 that the
rMr. White (Middlesex East).]
federal government took in by way of taxes about $4,509 million, or 67 per cent of all the tax moneys paid. In the province of Ontario the province got about 20 per cent, and the municipalities $900 million or 13 per cent. I understand that over the years the municipalities' percentage has been reduced to about 11 per cent.
I have some resolutions from some municipalities in the province of Ontario dealing with this question of dominion, provincial and municipal share of taxes. This is a resolution from the city of London, dated May 14, 1956. It says:
Whereas the last quarter century has seen great changes in the living standards of the people of Canada;
And whereas these changes have increased the variation in the personal income of the citizens;
And whereas the increased standards demand more and more public services both material and cultural;
And whereas the municipal governments are asked to supply many of those services from taxes based on values unrelated to modern incomes;
And whereas the municipal percentage of the total taxes paid has dropped from 29 per cent to 11 per cent despite the fact that mill rates have increased while provincial and federal rates have decreased;
Those are the factors presented in the resolution to bring to the attention of the authorities the plight of the city of London and the municipality of Long Branch near the city of Toronto. Last year the city of London paid $150,000 in sales tax to the senior government.
I just want to read one paragraph of another resolution of May 24, 1955:
And whereas this problem has been drawn to the attention of the dominion government on many occasions and, notwithstanding assurances that the submissions of this and other municipalities would be studied during the preparation of the annual budget of the dominion government, no action has been taken to afford relief to the municipalities of Canada by way of exemption from sales tax.
Here is one municipality that pays $150,000 in one year into the coffers of the government. I suppose the minister will reply by saying, "Well, we have to get the money somewhere", but it seems to me that this is a type of, shall I say, double taxation that puts an unfair burden on the home owner in the municipality.
Let me read one paragraph from the submission of the city of Fort William:
The high cost of financing capital improvements is threatening and seriously curtailing the expansion program of many municipalities in Ontario.
Then the survey commenced by the United Nations has this to say:
Wages, salaries in Canada rose 4] times, 1935 to 1952, and government spending six times.
Therefore the actual squeeze of taxes becomes greater and greater as time goes on.

Then the minister will recall that very recently the president of Stelco had this to say. I can remember when they were talking of taxes to control inflation. They were going to draw off surplus purchasing power in the hands of the consumers, but the president of Stelco does not go along with this idea. He said:
It is difficult to understand the argument that high taxes curb inflation, H. G. Hilton, president of Steel Company of Canada Limited, said today at the company's annual meeting.
"What difference can it make as far as inflation is concerned," asked Mr. Hilton, "if we as individuals spend or save our money as we see fit, or if our governments take it from us and spend it as they see fit?"
I think that answers in a way the claim that governments are taxing to help control inflation. In a sense it sometimes adds to inflation.
Along with other hon. members who have taken part in this debate, I was hoping that out of those conferences that have been held and the many things that have been said about them pro and con, probably some equitable solution to the problem would be found; and I think we shall hear more and more of this as time goes on.

Mr. Chairman, at this stage in an 11-hour day I daresay that the keen edge of the minister's mind and his receptivity to suggestion or even to constructive criticism are somewhat dulled, so I shall begin by giving him the best of my thoughts on his resolution and save perhaps the more critical remarks for the morning.
It appears to me that the principles on which the minister justifies the resolution in the addresses he made on it are principles which everyone would accept. Perhaps the difference will be in the application of those principles. I refer to the first of those basic considerations for which he was striving, as enunciated in an earlier speech, and that was to make revenues available to the provinces consistent with their responsibilities. I am sure that is what every member of the house wants to secure by any federal-provincial arrangement, an assurance that the provinces will have the means of carrying out their responsibilities.
Then the next principle was that of maintenance of full employment. I think the minister said maintenance of a high level of employment. That is a theory that was raised with very considerable enthusiasm by all governments and parties some years ago and subscribed to with a great deal of zest on the hustings and in the House of Commons; and it is, of course, a much to be desired end.
16. 1956	6043
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements
The third reason behind this scheme of federal-provincial agreements was that of simplicity in collection, which all taxpayers appreciate; and equity, I think the minister said, to the taxpayer. I daresay the ends which he would define as being his ends are those that I myself think are desirable; that is, a strong central government with adequate resources to carry out its obligations, and strong and independent provinces with adequate resources to carry out their obligations. The real problem is how to achieve both of these results in an effective and harmonious way. I suggest that the basic test by which this resolution should be judged and by which the bill should be analysed when it comes before the house is whether it does tend to the maintenance of the confederation, of the federal principle of government.
Some people may ask, why should we maintain the federal principle of government? I do not think the minister is one of those. All of us recognize that times change and that there is a need for change in any constitution or in any system such as our federal system, and that from time to time there is a shift in emphasis with a change in the economy. Therefore since 1867 we have seen a great many conferences just like the one which recently concluded. I think there have been 17 interprovincial and federal-provincial conferences in all, and if one counted the conference which began on July 9 in the Atlantic province, the conference among the four premiers of the Atlantic provinces perhaps we could count 18. They have been ample proof of the need for reconsideration of the basis on which responsibilities and revenues have been adjusted in our federal system.
But the basic factors which were present in 1867 are as pressing and vital today as they were then. I think those factors are that Canada is a country of two races, two languages, two cultures; that there is diversity, and there needs to be local government to satisfy the needs of diverse groups. There is in addition the diversity of our geographical location and division, which does not need to be recalled to this house because it has often been mentioned. Those diversities are as real as they were then and need recognition today as they did in 1867.
The problem is to create unity in the face of so much adversity, as has been said by Professor Corry of Queen's University in a very apt phrase. While a substantial part of Canada desires local autonomy-and there is no question that the substantial part of Canada does desire local autonomy-it is clear that the federal system has not outlived its usefulness and is the only means
6044	HOUSE OF
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements by which we can achieve unity in this country. I think no one who speaks the French language would deny that over 30 per cent of Canadians ardently desire the right to be different. That seems to me to be the conclusion of all sound opinion; therefore, as I suggest, it is the basic test which should be applied to this resolution and to the bill which is to follow it.
There are two aspects to the resolution which the minister has presented, and they are separate, distinct and different in principle. The first aspect is that of the division of taxing powers, and you might call that the arrangement for the renting of tax fields or the sharing of tax fields, depending on where the emphasis is put. The emphasis has shifted since 1946. In 1946, when Mr. Ilsley introduced his budget after an unsuccessful attempt to reach an agreement among the provinces, the emphasis was on the central authority renting from the provinces their major tax fields; and those tax rental agreements which were entered into by most of the provinces at that time gave way in due course to a further series of agreements with a slight shift in emphasis. Now in 1956-57 the agreements are running out and a new arrangement must be found.
Despite the fact that these agreements have not met with acceptance by any of the provinces I think it is fair to say there has been decided progress in the approach the minister has made and in the ingenious development of the theory which has been developing over the course of 10 years. I would like to acknowledge the ingenuity and skill of the members of that great department of government who have devised the new formula.
The improvement which I acknowledge tonight and suggest exists here is that there is now greater evidence than there has been in the past of a desire to share those fields which are the property of both the provinces and the dominion. The emphasis in the past has been more on keeping control of those tax fields by the dominion and paying the provinces some subsidy by way of rental for the use of the fields, but one can see here that there has been an effort to achieve a balance between the two ideas of the rental of the tax fields to the federal government and the joint occupation of those tax fields or the sharing of them between the two levels of government.
The other aspect of the proposed agreement is that of subsidy, and it takes its form here in equalization payments. That is not a new

idea, as I shall indicate a little later on, but it is a vitally necessary part of the fiscal arrangements between the federal government and the provinces. It has been recognized since the time of the earliest agreements that some subsidies were necessary and some such payments had to be made to those parts of Canada and those governments which perhaps gained less from confederation; or shall we say, using the words of some of them, "suffered more from confederation" than others, and therefore had to be compensated to put them in a position of equality with the others.
We have had constant reminders of the feeling that certain parts of Canada have contributed more to and received less from this union. We have even had suggestions of secession from time to time, but perhaps they have not been too serious. I reemember that one wag gave a name to the secessionist movement in Alberta and British Columbia a few years ago. He suggested that when that part of Canada broke away the two provinces in their united form might very well be called "Albumbia". There have been rumblings in the maritimes from time to time, and it is not clear yet whether confederation has been accepted in the newest province, Newfoundland.
In any event I think our objective in trying to work out a new fiscal arrangement within the federal system is to allay as much as possible these feelings of injustice which to the minds of us on this side of the house appear to be pretty strong and rather widespread.
As I understand the position, the minister comes to the house with a resolution, but he is not in a position to say that if we pass the resolution and the bill any of the provinces will welcome it as a solution to their problem.
Mr. Chairman, it is ten o'clock.
Progress reported.
